articles.title_orig: President Xi Jinping Meets with Singaporean Prime Minister Lawrence Wong
articles.title_zh: President Xi Jinping Meets with Singaporean Prime Minister Lawrence Wong
articles.source: 中华人民共和国驻美利坚合众国大使馆
articles.content_orig:
On the morning of November 20, 2026, Chinese President Xi Jinping met in Shenzhen with Singaporean Prime Minister Lawrence Wong, who is in China for the APEC Economic Leadersâ Meeting.
President Xi noted that China and Singapore, as close, friendly neighbors and important development partners, have achieved fruitful outcomes in exchanges and cooperation across all fields and delivered tangible benefits to the two peoples. With momentous changes unseen in a century accelerating across the globe, China and Singapore should grasp the trend of the times, strengthen strategic communication, enhance solidarity and coordination, and continuously take the China-Singapore all-round high-quality future-oriented partnership to new levels, with a view to better serving the modernization endeavors of both sides and making positive contributions to the prosperity and stability of the region and beyond.
President Xi emphasized that China and Singapore should be sincere friends that trust each other, cement political mutual trust, uphold common interests, and support each other in pursuing a development path suited to their respective national conditions. China and Singapore should be each otherâs development partners in spearheading innovation. The two sides should continue to promote highâquality Belt and Road cooperation, operate major cooperation projects to a high standard, commence negotiations for ChinaâSingapore Free Trade Agreement 4.0 upgrade, and deliver signature cooperation outcomes in digital economy, green development, and artificial intelligence to promote innovationâdriven, smart and green transition in bilateral cooperation. China and Singapore should be close, friendly neighbors of mutual learning, and work to deepen experience sharing on governance, enhance interâparty cooperation, and expand peopleâtoâpeople exchanges, with a view to cementing public support for friendship between the two sides. China and Singapore should be a force for progress that upholds international fairness and justice, and work to enhance coordination and collaboration within APEC, ChinaâASEAN cooperation frameworks and in other multilateral fora, steer East Asia cooperation in the right direction and safeguard regional peace and stability, with a view to building an AsiaâPacific community and a community with a shared future for humanity.
Prime Minister Wong said that Singapore and China enjoy ever deepening cooperation across all areas and a robust all-round partnership. Singapore firmly adheres to the one-China policy and opposes âTaiwan Independence.â Singapore highly values the Singapore-China partnership. It is ready to work with China to enhance political mutual trust, strengthen exchanges at all levels and cooperation in trade, industrial and supply chains, and artificial intelligence, and promote people-to-people exchanges in a bid to steadily advance bilateral relations. China successfully hosted the APEC Economic Leadersâ Meeting in Shenzhen. The vision for openness, innovation, and cooperation advocated by China meets the development needs of the Asia-Pacific region. Singapore congratulates China on hosting the China-Russia-U.S. summit, which is of great significance amid the turbulent and changing international environment and is conducive to upholding world peace and stability. The Singaporean side supports the vision of building a community with a shared future for humanity and the four global initiatives proposed by President Xi Jinping, and is ready to enhance communication and cooperation with China on international affairs to jointly address global challenges.ââ
Cai Qi, Wang Yi, Huang Kunming and others were at the meeting.

articles.title_orig: Why China is unwilling to be the world's next climate leader
articles.title_zh: Why China is unwilling to be the world's next climate leader
articles.content_orig:
Add Axios as your preferred source to
see more of our stories on Google.
Illustration: Brendan Lynch/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
Every year, tens of thousands of people gather to discuss nothing short of humanity's future on a hotter planet. Yet the world seems increasingly distracted by just about everything else.
Why it matters: For all of their flaws, these annual gatherings remain one of the few places where the world collectively confronts a problem that no country can solve alone.
Driving the news: The annual United Nations climate summit enters its final stretch this week in Antalya, Turkey, with negotiators trying to bridge disagreements over fossil fuels, clean electricity and money to help poorer countries confront climate change.
The big picture: Climate diplomacy hasn't been futile. Nor has it been sufficient. The landmark Paris Climate Agreement in 2015, which aimed to limit global warming to well below 2 degrees Celsius, helped usher in an era of climate progress.
State of play: Climate change isn't waiting patiently for its turn in the world's crowded list of priorities.
Catch up fast: Wildfires choked communities across Washington state and Europe with destruction and smoke this past summer.
Reality check: Just a few other things seem more urgent. Take your pick:
Yes, but: Life never allows us to work through our problems one by one. It's like someone with diabetes getting into a car accident. The accident demands immediate attention, but the diabetes still needs to be managed long after that acute accident has passed.
By the numbers: The World Economic Forum's annual survey of global risks captures this tension rather perfectly.
How it works: In the climate biz, these gatherings are known as COPs, short for Conferences of the Parties. It's a wonky acronym that virtually everyone outside the climate world might assume has to do with police.
Zoom in: This year's gathering is tackling two issues increasingly central to the world's economy: artificial intelligence and electrification.
Friction point: Criticism is almost as perennial as the conference itself: It's insular. It's outdated. It doesn't have the right people at the table. It's painfully bureaucratic.
Between the lines: A COP's importance is often measured by how many people attend and who shows up, with more than 120 U.S. state and local leaders going this year.
Zoom out: Every COP is like a snowflake: specifically different but broadly the same. I've attended four (though not this year's in Turkey).
Flashback: In Marrakesh in 2016, I felt like I'd arrived at the coolest climate party a year too late, after the Paris Agreement.
The bottom line: It's often hard to decipher progress from one COP to the next, but the cumulative impact over decades is what matters. And in a world with no shortage of distractions, climate change isn't going anywhere.

articles.title_orig: U.S.-China trade, Taiwan and tech tensions remain unresolved as Trump returns from Asia
articles.title_zh: U.S.-China trade, Taiwan and tech tensions remain unresolved as Trump returns from Asia
articles.content_orig:
SHENZHEN, China — Even as Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders gathered for high-profile photos at the summit's close, key issues from Nvidia to Taiwan remained unaddressed.
"The intrigue is around not what was said, but what remains unresolved," said Gary Dvorchak, managing director at Blueshirt.
"Taiwan remains a major source of strategic uncertainty. North Korea was notably absent from the trilateral nuclear declaration," he said. "Southeast Asia, which is increasingly central to global manufacturing and investment, was overshadowed by major-power diplomacy."
President Donald Trump did not meet with North Korea's leader Kim Jong Un, despite speculation .
Taiwan, one of the 21 member economies of APEC, sent Acer Group founder and honorary chairman Stan Shih to Shenzhen. But the self-governed island, which Beijing claims is part of its territory, did not feature in any significant way during the event. Taiwan is set to hold key elections for Taipei mayor and other posts on Nov. 28.
Instead, the highlight of this week's APEC summit in Shenzhen was a trilateral meeting Thursday between Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin . The three leaders, meeting together for the first time, reaffirmed interests in reducing nuclear risks and plans to increase oil production.
"The optics are impressive, but there's not much happening," Ian Bremmer, president and founder of Eurasia Group, said Friday of the trilateral on CNBC's " Squawk Box Asia ."
Resolving the years-long Ukraine war would require involvement from President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European allies, Bremmer said.
Ahead of the trilateral, Trump and Xi also held their third bilateral summit of the year. Xi greeted Trump at the airport late Wednesday, reciprocating the hospitality shown in September when the Chinese leader visited Washington.
But little was shared publicly on whether the two countries agreed to reduce tariffs further, allow rare earths to keep flowing beyond a January deadline, or address tech competition.
Recent reports tying Jensen Huang to an alleged Chinese spy led to the executive's resignation as Nvidia CEO. It also raised questions in Congress about the effectiveness of U.S. efforts to restrict China's access to advanced chips used to train artificial intelligence.
Trump indicated to Fox News that Nvidia came up briefly in his talks with Xi. U.S. officials last week said Trump did not plan to raise the matter, while noting Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk would accompany the U.S. president.
No other executive was named. Other American business leaders, including Visa CEO Ryan McInerney, who also chairs the U.S.-China Business Council, joined the APEC CEO Summit and was seen at a welcome banquet Wednesday evening .
However, Musk did not appear with Trump at major APEC-related events. CNBC was present for the opening portions of a banquet Wednesday and the Economic Leaders' Meeting Thursday and did not see Musk.
In fact, Musk flew to Shanghai Thursday morning to visit Tesla's factory there, a company executive said on Chinese social media . Musk also showed up in a social media video with Ren Hongbin, chairman of the China Council for the Promotion of International Trade.
Musk addressed Wednesday's DealBook Summit in New York via video conference, having previously said on X that he would be joining from China.
Tesla and the White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment.
"We still don't have a durable resolution of the U.S.-China trade dispute," Dvorchak said, adding: "Business needs certainty, not just ceremony."
Trump visited Shenzhen after briefly traveling to the Philippines on Tuesday for a meeting with the leaders of Australia, India and Japan as part of the Quad grouping happening on the sidelines of the ASEAN Summit. Trump also met the prime minister of Thailand, Anutin Charnvirakul.
Topics of discussion included U.S. cooperation with the region, trade and critical minerals, U.S. Ambassador to ASEAN Kevin Kim told reporters Wednesday. He declined to comment on whether China's influence in the region was addressed.
Kim emphasized it was the second year in a row that Trump visited Southeast Asia, and noted the region "will be at the heart of SI [artificial intelligence] going forward," making it important that American technology is "getting into the right hands" through a regulatory framework the president is building.
Speaking to reporters a day later in Shenzhen, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi also highlighted the ASEAN and Quad events over APEC. "The major outcome of this diplomatic week was the Quad Summit," she said, noting via official English translation how the four leaders expressed " strong opposition to the unilateral approach to change the status quo by force or coercion ... [as well as] arbitrary export control."
Takaichi, the first Japanese leader in seven years to visit China, received a cool reception upon her arrival in Shenzhen for the APEC meeting.
Tensions between Japan and China have escalated since Takaichi drew Beijing's ire in Nov. 2025 when she said that a Chinese attack on Taiwan could draw a Japanese military response.
Takaichi said Thursday that Japan's position on Taiwan remained unchanged as stated in the 1972 Japan-China Communiqué.
The communique said Japan "understands and respects" the People's Republic of China's position on Taiwan, but does not explicitly acknowledge Taiwan as part of the PRC.
— CNBC's Anniek Bao and Lim Hui Jie contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Rep. John Moolenaar: Nvidia, AMD chip sales to China need scrutiny
articles.title_zh: Rep. John Moolenaar: Nvidia, AMD chip sales to China need scrutiny
articles.content_orig:
The subagency of the Commerce Department that regulates and enforces exports approved the sale of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies including Alibaba and Tencent as of May 2026, according to documents released Thursday by the House Foreign Affairs Committee.
Some of those approvals, made by Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, included sales to companies designated by the Department of Defense as "Chinese Military Companies," according to the documents. From December through May, companies had made 3.4 million requests for sales of U.S. AI chips to China, the committee reported, citing those made by Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices .
"Over the past month, the administration's handling of chip export controls has put our national security and technology edge at risk. The Bureau of Industry and Security has failed to enforce the rules, and Congress must now conduct rigorous oversight of the administration's policies," Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said at a meeting of the panel Thursday at which members voted to release the documents.
Spokespersons for Nvidia and AMD said their companies comply with U.S. export control laws.
Nvidia argued it was following the Commerce Department regulations that were in effect at the time.
A spokesperson from the Bureau of Industry and Security said it shared information with Congress on both approvals and denials of licenses for Nvidia's H200 and comparable chips. "Licensing decisions are the product of deliberation and consultation among multiple U.S. Government agencies," the spokesperson said.
"The review and licensing process spanned more than half a year, with approvals subject to strict conditions and limited volumes. Despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to China," Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo told CNBC.
On Tuesday, Nvidia reported $2.4 billion in quarterly revenue from H200 and related chip sales in China. In total, customers based in China and Hong Kong made up about 9.5% of all revenue.
"AMD complies with applicable U.S. export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations," AMD said through a spokesperson.
The approval of 879,000 AI chips is "not that many," Bernstein Senior Analyst Stacy Rasgon told CNBC, adding that this news is not surprising.
"It doesn't sound to me like they're approving everything they got willy nilly," Rasgon said of the Commerce Department. With 879,000 approvals out of 3.4 million requested AI chip sales, he added, "There was a process in place, and it sounds like they approved about one out of every four."
Despite a rapid succession of China export controls on AI chips that started under the Biden administration in 2022, Nvidia and AMD both re-engineered some chips to comply and be sold legally in China. And in December, Trump said Nvidia could ship H200s, its older generation Hopper chips, to "approved customers in China" if the U.S. got a 25% cut of sales.
The U.S. then licensed Nvidia H200 sales to Alibaba , Tencent, ByteDance and other Chinese companies, although sales were limited because Beijing didn't approve large-scale imports, chip analyst Patrick Moorhead of Moor Insights & Strategy told CNBC last week.
H200 sales numbers remained low due to those restrictions on China's end. Nvidia said H200 shipments to China made up less than 1% of data center revenue for the quarter that ended in July.
"In the grand context of the size of this market and how much they're shipping, it's a rounding error. It's tiny," Rasgon told CNBC.
The committee cited the Export Control Reform Act as justification for releasing the data. The panel said the law allows it to declassify and release export data if it "determines that the withholding of the following information is contrary to the national interest."
The license requests released by the Foreign Affairs Committee include requests to sell to major firms including ByteDance, Tesla (Shanghai) and Baidu .
The release of documents comes in the wake of Jensen Huang 's resignation from the chip supplier Nvidia after news surfaced that he had several extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy that led to concerns about Nvidia chips being diverted to China.
In the weeks since, Republicans and Democrats in Congress have called for legislation to be passed that would impose stricter export controls on the sale of advanced AI chips to China and other adversaries.
"The license information we are disclosing today will help inform the American public about how BIS has handled licenses for Nvidia H200 and equivalent AMD chips to China. The public has the right to know how these decisions were made," Meeks said.
Mast said two of the firms listed in Nvidia license applications to BIS —  Maginfra and New Matrix — are suspected "smuggling fronts." The New York Times reported in November that both companies had empty offices and had ties to companies under national security sanctions.
"Both are fake companies. If BIS approved the sale of these chips to these firms, obviously that is of tremendous concern to us — especially given that President Trump made clear last year that the sale of any AI chips to China will have very real national security conditions," Mast said at the Thursday meeting.
Maginfra and New Matrix did not reply to requests for comment.
Shares of AMD fell Thursday after the investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging the company "has its own China problem." The report claims that "after the U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems, the company kept getting newer AMD firmware, which enables AMD chips to run in servers."
CNBC did not independently verify this information.
Fallout from the Huang scandal on Capitol Hill has intensified in the last week, as lawmakers question the degree to which the former head of Nvidia's relationship with the suspected Chinese spy could have jeopardized national security and American AI dominance.
Huang is due for a closed-door transcribed interview with the House Foreign Affairs panel and two other committees on Dec. 1. Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter is scheduled to appear before the panels Dec. 2.
Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., announced on CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had also agreed to testify.
Lutnick has come under fire over his relationship to Huang and for his failure to take action on Megaspeed , the Singaporean company where Alice Huang , with whom the former Nvidia CEO had an affair, was an executive until 2025. U.S. investigators suspect Megaspeed diverted Nvidia chips to China.
Amid that criticism, the Commerce Department on Monday issued an interim final rule to close a loophole that has allowed Chinese companies to lease Nvidia's advancing computing power from data centers in third countries.
The rule was "written by and at the direction of" the Treasury Department and the White House National Security Council, BIS said in a press release.
— Megan Cassella , Daren Fonda and Kif Leswing contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: U.S. Has Floated NATO Membership for Ukraine in Recent Meetings
articles.title_zh: U.S. Has Floated NATO Membership for Ukraine in Recent Meetings
articles.content_orig:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has asked the United States to clarify what an Article 5-like security guarantee would mean for his country in a post-war scenario, warning that a new Russian attack is not a matter of "if" but of "when".
"I'm not sure we have a common acceptance of Article 5," Zelenskyy said on Thursday evening after a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing in Berlin.
The idea of developing a security guarantee for Ukraine modelled under NATO's collective defence, which states that an armed attack against one ally shall be considered an attack against all of them, was first raised in December of last year. However, the proposal was never fully developed as peace negotiations subsequently stalled.
It came back into focus on Thursday, as European leaders gathered in Berlin.
US special envoy Jared Kushner, who took part in the meeting, said President Donald Trump was "open" to providing such a commitment to a post-war Ukraine.
"From an American perspective, giving an Article 5-like security guarantee is a really, really big deal," Kushner said, speaking next to Zelenskyy.
"Obviously, it has to be in America's interest to do that. And we also have to make sure that it's part of a broader security package."
Kushner claimed that Russia has become "comfortable" with the concept, though he admitted "there's a lot of scepticism and disbelief" about it in Moscow. Kushner also said the Russian intention is "to not have another war in the future".
"That's why it's important to restart the dialogue between Europe and Russia," he said.
"We have to work on a system of incentives and interests to make sure that whatever agreement we come to is something that will be kept, it will be monitored, there'll be huge deterrence, and there'll be massive consequences if it's ever violated."
But in a subsequent press conference, Zelenskyy challenged the vagueness of Kushner's response, asking for specific details such as the possible deployment of US troops or the establishment of US bases on Ukrainian soil.
"What about American soldiers?" he said. "Do you have an answer on it? Me not. For today. I don't know the answer."
For an Article 5-like guarantee to work in practice, he said, the US and Europe have to properly spell out how they would react to a new Russian assault.
"What will partners do?" he said. "What happens if – sorry to be sceptical – not if, but when (Russians) will try to do it again? What will they do?"
"It has to be clear not only to partners (but also) to people, societies, investors" who will come to Ukraine after the war, he went on.
"All these people, they need clear answers."
Zelenskyy said that full-time NATO membership, a long-held goal for Kyiv and a red line for Moscow, would make it clearer, as his country would automatically benefit from the real Article 5 provision, the linchpin of the alliance's deterrence.
Ukraine's NATO dream has split allies, with some arguing it would be the easiest way to avoid a new invasion and others warning it would unnecessarily provoke Russia.
French President Emmanuel Macron said on Thursday that Russia's "maximalist" demands warranted revisiting "the question of Ukraine's NATO accession".
The meeting in Berlin ended with a declaration signed by Germany, France and the UK that featured a subtle reference to a potential Article 5-like security guarantee.
The text did not describe it as such, but as "a legally binding commitment, subject to national procedures, to take measures to restore peace and security in the case of a future armed attack by Russia".

articles.title_orig: U.S. and Israel considering new assault on Iran, sources say
articles.title_zh: U.S. and Israel considering new assault on Iran, sources say
articles.content_orig:
Tel Aviv — Israel and the U.S. are considering launching a new assault on Iran in the short term, according to sources familiar with the matter.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's administration is concerned about how rapidly the Iranians are rebuilding their ballistic missile manufacturing capabilities and the pace at which Iran is working to shield its military and nuclear infrastructure from attack by moving it underground, the sources told CBS News.
President Trump also said this week that Iran may be seeking to develop chemical or biological weapons, though he provided no evidence to support the claim.
Months of indirect negotiations between the U.S. and Iran have failed to bring a ceasefire deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and Iran has refused to even discuss its nuclear program unless the U.S. lifts its naval blockade and accepts six other key conditions .
Israel's military is prepared for a new round of fighting with Iran and is in peak defensive posture to respond to any first attack by Iran, the sources told CBS News.
The Netanyahu administration would prefer to launch a new joint operation with the U.S., but the sources told CBS News it remains unclear whether Mr. Trump wants to order new military action, and if so, what kind. The war was a key factor in the Republicans' defeat in the recent midterm elections and it remains deeply unpopular with Americans.
The U.S. has significant firepower in the region, including tens of thousands of forces and two aircraft carriers with their associated strike groups, amounting to dozens of warships and aircraft.
For both Mr. Trump and Netanyahu, who jointly launched the war with Iran almost nine months ago with a massive round of strikes on the Islamic Republic, the window for any new collaborative action may be closing.
Netanyahu could lose his position as prime minister in the coming weeks due to the results of Israel's national election late last month. Mr. Trump's Republican party will lose control of both houses of the U.S. Congress in January, meanwhile, giving his political opponents far greater say over financing of the war.
Neither Netanyahu's office nor Israel's military responded to CBS News' requests for comment on the planning for any renewed attacks on Iran, which would be the third round of major hostilities. The White House and U.S. military declined to comment on the current thinking within the administration, but American military commanders have long said they are prepared to execute any orders Mr. Trump gives. With the assets already in place a new offensive operation could be mounted within two to four days, if such an order were given.
Mr. Trump has said repeatedly that Iran is keen to make a deal to end the war, but Tehran has rejected any ceasefire to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, or any talks on its nuclear program, unless the U.S. agrees to seven key demands , including an end to hostilities on all fronts in the Middle East and an end of the U.S. blockade of Iran's ports and vessels.
Alongside the rising concern over Iran's growing capacity to produce conventional weapons — which the regime has boasted of itself —   President Trump also raised the possibility of the Islamic Republic working to obtain biological or chemical weapons.
"They're looking at gases, looking at bio, because we've shut them out with the nuclear," Mr. Trump told a Fox News reporter in China ahead of his meeting with his Russian and Chinese counterparts .
Iran's foreign ministry rejected the allegations on Thursday, comparing it to U.S. claims that Iraq was developing weapons of mass destruction before the invasion launched by then-President George W. Bush in 2003.
"We find ourselves facing ominous new allegations and a narrative that appears to be following the same fraudulent script," Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei said in a post on X .
President Trump has offered no clear signal about whether he intends to order major new military action against Iran. He told Fox News on Wednesday that he still wanted to reach a deal with Iran, but one that he feels will last, and also renewed his threat to use force.
"I'm going to finish it off ," Mr. Trump said of the war. "Yeah, soon. I mean, one way or the other, we'll finish it off."
On Thursday, however, he told Israel's Channel 12 that he's "not rushing into any decision," indicating a willingness, not for the first time, to let the stalemate drag on into 2027.
"We will see what happens after the beginning of the year," he told the television network.
U.S. Central Command chief Adm. Brad Cooper, who oversees American forces in the Middle East, met with top Israeli security officials at Israel's defense ministry Wednesday for what the Israeli military called a "joint, comprehensive situational assessment."
Israel's most senior general, Eyal Zamir, as well as the director of the Mossad intelligence agency, Roman Gofman, were among the senior Israeli officials who met with Cooper.
Israeli authorities confirming the Mossad director's attendance at the meeting was unusual, and many in the country have taken it as a sign that Iran was a key topic of discussion.
Gofman met U.S. officials in Washington last week, including CIA Director John Ratcliffe, according to people familiar with the matter.
"The head of the Mossad, who hardly leaves the country, didn't go for a brief in and out, but for a couple of days. It's a serious matter on the table," said Erez Winner, chairman of the Israel Defense and Security Forum, an Israeli think tank with close ties to the Netanyahu administration.
If the decision is made to take Israel back to war with Iran, it would come at a politically sensitive time for Netanyahu.
His political rivals, in the wake of last month's election, have been tasked with forming a government, potentially leaving him in power for just a few more weeks, possibly less.
Since losing his majority in Israel's parliament, Netanyahu has made the argument to his rivals, and to the Israeli public, that a unity government is required to deal with the country's pressing security threats. He has long accused Iran of having ambitions to build nuclear weapons, and placed that at the pinnacle of those threats.
Iran has always denied any desire to build nuclear weapons, though after President Trump pulled the U.S. out of a previous international nuclear agreement during his first term, it has enriched uranium to a point far beyond the needs of civilian nuclear programs.
International monitors believe Iran still has a stockpile of about 900 pounds of uranium enriched to 60% purity somewhere under the rubble of its heavily damaged nuclear facilities. At that level, the material is just a short technological step away from being enriched to weapons-grade.
Despite the concerns, some of Netanyahu's political rivals believe he is trying to take the country back to war to avoid losing power. In recent days, he has held security briefings with some of those rivals — an unusual step that analysts say may hint at the possibility of imminent military action.
President Trump endorsed Netanyahu before the Israeli election, and he said he also would prefer to pair up with the right-wing Israeli leader in any new attack on Iran.
The speculation about a major new operation comes amid a renewed tit-for-tat exchange of fire between Iran and the U.S.
The U.S. launched a strike on Iran's strategic Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, which American officials categorized as self-defense in response to Iranian strikes targeting U.S. assets in Bahrain, which the U.S. military said were intercepted. Iran has also launched strikes against Kuwait this week, with officials saying they caused no damage.
The Iranian regime has been preparing, publicly, for renewed hostilities, and it has warned that its response to any new attack would reach farther than its previous actions.

articles.title_orig: Rejecting cheap fabrics, higher prices: Why shoppers are asking for better clothes
articles.title_zh: Rejecting cheap fabrics, higher prices: Why shoppers are asking for better clothes
articles.content_orig:
Clothing isn't made like it used to be, and more shoppers are taking notice.
The makeup of apparel imported into the U.S. has shifted in recent years. In 2010, about 60% of clothing was predominantly made from cotton. Now, that total is around 45%, while predominantly synthetic fabrics such as polyester and nylon comprise the majority of imports.
Apparel prices generally declined over the two decades leading up to the pandemic, according to the consumer price index. Since 2020, they have soared to record highs.
It's starting to change habits for consumers who are paying more for food, gas, rent and other staples. As shoppers shell out more for clothes, they're increasingly making sure the garments are worth the cost.
Consulting firm AlixPartners' 2026 Consumer Sentiment Index, which surveyed more than 9,000 shoppers, found that consumers are scrutinizing labels more closely and rejecting cheap materials sold at a premium.
"If it's not a natural material, a retailer brand who passes it off as it is, they're really becoming very low on consumers' minds," said Sonia Lapinsky, head of fashion at AlixPartners.
Fast fashion brands like Forever 21 and H&M exploded in popularity during the early 2000s and 2010s, bringing trendy clothing to shelves quickly at low prices. Then came ultra-fast fashion, with brands like Shein and Fashion Nova pumping out new garments at even quicker speeds and lower price points — made possible in part through the use of inexpensive, synthetic fabrics.
"We got to a point where the pendulum just swung too far in that direction. And we've actually begun to see a reversal," said U.S. Bancorp BTIG consumer analyst Janine Stichter. "Quality matters a lot more ... over the last three or four years than it has in the previous 10 or 20."
But quality, which shoppers often tie directly to material, can come at a higher cost.
The average unit price of apparel imported to the U.S. between January and August was $2.64 per square meter for garments that were predominantly synthetic fiber, like polyester and nylon, compared with $3.67 for items that were largely cotton, according to data from the U.S. Commerce Department's Office of Textiles and Apparel.
When comparing those 2026 figures to 2010, synthetic fiber apparel import costs have climbed around 11%, while cotton apparel costs have risen 21%.
"If you're appealing to a more value-sensitive customer, you either reduce the quality, or you negotiate with suppliers to try to share some of the cost or you maybe absorb the cost … and perhaps hope to crank a higher volume of product to make up for it," said Bernstein Research senior retail analyst Aneesha Sherman.
Though polyester is cheaper, experts point out that's not necessarily a bad thing. It can help clothing hold its shape and wick away sweat.
Sherman believes the athleisure boom is a primary factor in the shift toward polyester. She said that from 2015 to 2025, sports apparel was growing at a 4.9% rate in the U.S., versus 2.6% for all apparel and footwear, according to Euromonitor data.
"There probably is some quality trade down as well happening there," Sherman said. "But I think both these trends are conflated."
Nonetheless, backlash to synthetic materials is growing. Gen Z has even repurposed the word "polyester" as an insult to mean generally low-quality or fake.
Concerns have also grown about the environment and human health surrounding petroleum-based clothing, as more research indicates microplastics can leach from polyester clothing when washed.
It's led consumers to reexamine what materials are in their clothing.
Apparel prices have risen coming out of the pandemic, as demand outpaced supply and allowed companies to raise prices, said BTIG's Stichter. Tariffs and the Iran war followed, raising costs for businesses — and prices for consumers.
Petroleum is the basis of many synthetic fibers, and oil prices have skyrocketed since the start of the Iran war.
The same factors that helped drive up prices of clothing — Covid, tariffs and war — also affected clothing quality.
"Companies had to move around their supply chains in the post-Covid period," said Stichter. "They had to find ways to take costs out, and sometimes that meant using less expensive fabrics."
Those factors compounded a more-than-decade-long shift away from manufacturing in China.
Sheng Lu, a fashion and apparel studies professor at the University of Delaware, whose research focuses on the economics of the global textile industry, said China's established history with clothing production means it has higher-skilled workers, state-of-the-art-equipment and better material management compared with emerging manufacturing destinations such as Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and Cambodia.
"They mostly serve the value market and the mass market. And I think the reason why they're not ready to make higher-quality luxury and premium products really reflects the kind of skill sets you can expect when you source from these countries," said Lu.
AlixPartners' Lapinsky said these countries that manufacture at a lower cost sometimes have to still ship the raw materials from China, which can extend the timeline to make clothing. That means taking earlier bets on trends and then discounting if products don't sell well.
"If you have to mark down that product because the consumer doesn't want it as much, your net margin might actually be worse than if you were to just invest in quality in the first place," said BTIG's Stichter.
And as material costs rise for synthetic fibers, Stichter also said she believes it could further influence companies to use more natural fabrics moving forward.
Companies prioritizing quality are winning in this environment.
Ralph Lauren's stock is up around 85% over the past two years. Around 90% of its apparel is primarily made of cotton, leather, wool, viscose, cashmere or silk, according to its 2026 sustainability report. In its fiscal 2026, the company said it sold more products at full price and reduced markdowns.
Meanwhile, direct-to-consumer clothing brand Quince, which centers its brand identity around natural materials, reached a $10 billion valuation this year.
The brand jumped 16 spots to No. 3 for best resale value in online consignment retailer ThredUp's 2025 report . Organic cotton retailer Pact jumped 20 spots on that list to No. 8, illustrating the potential role materials are playing in brand recognition.
Alternatively, the 2026 AlixPartners report, which ranks sentiment for brands in different retail categories, found shoppers are viewing some fast fashion brands less favorably. Both Shein and Zara dropped three spots — to fifth and seventh place, respectively — in terms of sentiment in the young adult specialty category.
Shein passed higher tariff costs onto shoppers in 2025 and then blamed a sales slowdown on those higher prices . The ultra-fast fashion retailer saw its year-over-year share of U.S. apparel, accessories and footwear card spending decrease in the fourth quarter of 2025 and first two quarters of 2026, according to Consumer Edge .
Shein did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Though Zara fell in AlixPartners' Consumer Sentiment Index, it has continued to grow sales and profits year over year. Even so, Lapinsky said worsening consumer views are something to watch, even if the company is doing well.
"What we found over the years with this consumer sentiment index is that sometimes it will be a bit of a leading indicator of what's to come," said AlixPartners' Lapinsky. "I'm not saying that this is going to be true for Zara, but I think that's one thing that we'll be watching as we look in the upcoming quarters and into 2027."

articles.title_orig: Russia bombards Ukraine, killing at least 8 after Putin vowed retaliation for Kerch Bridge attack
articles.title_zh: Russia bombards Ukraine, killing at least 8 after Putin vowed retaliation for Kerch Bridge attack
articles.content_orig:
Russia launched a deadly attack on Ukraine overnight into Friday, hours after President Vladimir Putin met his US and Chinese counterparts for historic trilateral talks in which the three powers billed themselves as a force for peace in the world.
Trump spoke with European leaders after the call, reportedly describing Putin as “tired” and ready for peace. But Kyiv said Russia fired at least 110 missiles overnight - an unusually large number even amid Russia’s frequent aerial assaults.
Nine people have been killed and at least 28 injured during the missile and drone attack which lasted more than ten hours, according to Ukrainian authorities.
Some 400 drones, including 120 jet-powered drones which are essentially compact cruise missiles, were part of the attack.
The Polish government said Polish and NATO fighter jets were scrambled and Patriot air defense systems activated early on Friday after Poland’s airspace was violated during the attack, with “objects” flying in and falling inside the country’s territory.
Mark Rutte, NATO’s Secretary General, condemned the attack and its spillover into the alliance’s territory.
“This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine … we continue to stand united as Allies and will continue to support Ukraine,” he said in a statement.
The assault came hours after Putin left China following a day of meetings in Shenzhen with US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping.
The talks failed to produce any breakthrough in Moscow’s more than four-year war in Ukraine, and appeared to be used by Putin as an opportunity to repeat his maximalist demands in front of a global audience.
The Russian leader hailed the summit as historic and told reporters the discussions took place in a “relaxed and very intimate atmosphere.”
In his opening remarks, Putin said Russia, China and the US had “shared interests” in settling the Ukraine war.
No official declaration was released after the talks, but Trump did later speak with the so-called Coalition of the Willing, a group of Ukraine’s key allies, which was convening in Berlin with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
According to a senior European official with knowledge of the call’s contents, the president’s main message was that “Putin is tired, wants to end this, ready for a deal.”
The official said Trump’s suggestion was “to reach out and grasp at the opportunity.” He said the Europeans were “constructive in response but want proof.”
Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk, who was part of the call, said Trump sounded “fairly optimistic,” but he words were received “very cautiously in the room.”
“I don’t hide the fact that I’ve heard this very often from President Trump. His belief in Putin’s goodwill seems unshakable, even though so far there are no facts to support it,” he said, adding that it “would be good, if it really turned out that Russia was genuinely ready to engage in peace talks.”
Kushner said Trump had conveyed a “very strong message” to both Xi and Putin about his desire for peace and would like “to engage both of them very aggressively to get there.”
Russia’s defense ministry said in a post to Telegram it launched a “massive strike using high-precision weapons from land, sea, and air,” as well as drones, targeting Ukrainian military and energy facilities, port infrastructure in the Odesa region, and transport infrastructure in Kyiv.
But Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky said “absolutely all the targets were ordinary civilian infrastructure – things that literally sustain people’s lives.”
“This was one of the largest attacks. The strike tactics were particularly vicious this time: several groups of missiles were launched, with pauses of 20 to 30 minutes between them to make it harder to put out fires, clear rubble, and carry out repairs,” Zelensky said.
Zelensky said that 27 of the missiles Russia fired overnight were ballistic. According to the Ukrainian Air Force, only three were intercepted, reflecting Ukraine’s critical shortage of missiles for it US-made Patriot air defense system.
Earlier, Ukraine said Moscow’s targets included a hospital in Kharkiv and residential buildings in the Dnipropetrovsk, Lviv, Vinnytsia, Sumy, and Chernihiv regions.
Three of Kyiv’s bridges were damaged in the overnight strikes, according to mayor Vitaly Klitschko, halting transport links connecting the two sides of the capital.
“All emergency services have done and will continue to do everything possible to mitigate the consequences of the attack as quickly as possible,” Klitschko said, adding that people should avoid traveling if possible.
The deadly attack came after Putin vowed revenge for Ukraine’s recent attacks on prized project, the strategic multibillion-dollar bridge linking Russia with the occupied Crimea.
“There will be no negotiations,” he said. “I believe our response, as I have just said, will be far more painful than what the Kyiv regime did to the bridge.”
The attacks have also knocked down power in several regions across Ukraine, just as temperatures are beginning to drop to bellow zero.
Several districts in Kyiv were without power due to the attack, according to energy company DTEK. Emergency power outages have also been implemented in the Lviv, Zakarpattia, and Ivano-Frankivsk regions, according to Ukrenergo, the country’s state-owned electricity operator, which called the situation in the power grid “extremely critical.”
CNN’s Nick Paton Walsh, Clare Sebastian and Victoria Butenko contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Dems crash Elon Musk’s Texas honeymoon
articles.title_zh: Dems crash Elon Musk’s Texas honeymoon
articles.content_orig:
Gina Hinojosa, the governor-elect of the U.S. state of Texas, said clearly in an interview on Thursday that she does not oppose the data center industry, but stressed that a pause on new data center permits must remain in place until the state legislature passes legislation protecting residents' rights. She also extended an olive branch, saying she is willing to work with SpaceX CEO Elon Musk on data center issues, leaving room for negotiation in a policy battle that is swaying the outlook for AI-related trades.
Hinojosa defeated incumbent Governor Greg Abbott in the Nov. 3 midterm elections to become Texas's next governor and is expected to take office in January. During the campaign she repeatedly called for a pause on new data center development, stoking market concerns that Texas's data center construction boom could cool and ripple through the broader artificial intelligence investment chain.
Asked whether she would ban data center construction permits in the state, Hinojosa responded: "I don't hate data centers. I just hate the way they are currently taking advantage of the people of Texas." She elaborated that Texas currently lacks laws sufficient to protect residents, so her position is to pause the issuance of new data center permits until the relevant legislation is completed.
The remarks drew intense attention because Texas is already the core region of the current U.S. data center construction wave. According to a mid-2026 JLL report, Texas has a combined 26 gigawatts of existing and under-construction data center capacity, twice the 13 gigawatts of Virginia, another data center hub. The local power regulator has disclosed that 433 data center load projects have submitted materials, involving about 177 gigawatts of requested interconnection capacity, with potential demand far exceeding the current scale.
Regulatory Review Restarts; SpaceX Project Clears First
Before Hinojosa's remarks, Texas's regulatory environment had already loosened. A spokesperson for the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) said the agency received notice on Nov. 13 from Governor Abbott's office that the state's grid operator had completed gathering information on the community impact of pending data centers, ending what had been a de facto permitting pause.
Previously, Abbott had asked the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) to assess the potential risks of data center expansion to the state's grid and in September directed environmental regulators to pause issuing permits until the assessment was complete. The move reflected the growing tension between the AI infrastructure investment boom and the carrying capacity of local power and water resources; in many parts of the United States, data center expansion has been blamed for driving up residential electricity bills and became a hot issue in this year's midterm elections.
After the resumption of permitting, Musk's SpaceX Texas project was the first to make progress. On Nov. 16, TCEQ issued an air pollution emissions permit for the data center and supporting natural gas power plant SpaceX plans to build, clearing a major regulatory hurdle for the project with total investment of about $24 billion (about NT$790 billion). The project is located in southern Texas, adjacent to Starbase, where SpaceX is headquartered. Regulatory documents show SpaceX is authorized to use 43 behind-the-meter generating units and related emissions at the data center.
However, ERCOT's full review report has not yet been published. Complete findings on community impact and interconnection requests are expected to be submitted on Dec. 10 and discussed at a public meeting of the Public Utility Commission of Texas on Dec. 17.
Musk: Incoming Governor Is Moderate
Musk spent heavily in the midterms to support Republicans, and Texas is home to the headquarters of his Tesla and SpaceX. With Democrats winning the governor's race, shares of both companies have come under pressure recently.
Asked whether she had contacted Musk, Hinojosa said: "I have not talked to Elon Musk. I look forward to speaking with him at some point." She added that Musk has several businesses in Texas and that she looks forward to working with him, provided such cooperation aims to ensure Texans' lives improve and they prosper.
Hinojosa describes herself as an "economic populist" who believes government should put residents' interests first and that people want leaders who can withstand pressure from the business community. "We can have a strong business community. But first and foremost, the economy has to serve the people of Texas," she said.
On the other side, Musk's assessment of the new Democratic governor has trended positive. Speaking at a summit on Wednesday, he said: "Actually, I think the new governor is going to be quite moderate." He added: "I don't think she's a far-left governor. From everything I hear, I think Texas will do well with Gina as governor."
In a Nov. 13 interview, Hinojosa further clarified the policy boundaries: as long as a project still needs other state permits, the corresponding approvals will be paused, but she did not say she would revoke permits already granted. She also stressed that canceling state-level tax incentives for data centers alone is not enough; new rules must protect water resources and the grid and let local communities participate in deciding whether and how data centers are built.
Market Closely Watching Policy Continuity
For developers, Texas's resumption of environmental permit reviews amounts to reopening a regulatory gate, but whether the policy can continue is still the biggest variable. Jefferies analysts said in a report that developers are trying to gauge how long Texas's current data center permitting policy can last, and the policy signals from the governor-elect will be key.
Citi analysts believe TCEQ's resumption of permitting is a positive for projects planning to build their own power generation, but cautioned: "Getting an air emissions permit does not necessarily mean construction or grid connection will speed up."
On the policy timeline, the submission of ERCOT's full review report on Dec. 10, the Public Utility Commission's public meeting discussion on Dec. 17 and the new governor's inauguration in January will be three points to watch. Whether Texas can strike a balance between attracting AI computing investment and protecting residents' electricity bills and water resources will directly affect the investment plans of data center developers, power companies and related supply chains.

articles.title_orig: Russia accuses Estonia of erecting new 'Iron Curtain' with border closure, says it will respond
articles.title_zh: Russia accuses Estonia of erecting new 'Iron Curtain' with border closure, says it will respond
articles.content_orig:
MOSCOW, Nov 20 (Reuters) - Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova on Friday accused Estonia ‌of planning to erect a new "Iron ‌Curtain" and said it would respond after Estonia said it ​would close its border with Russia for at least six months.
Estonia's government's said on Friday it would close its road border crossings with Russia ‌on security grounds ⁠from December 1 and decide after six months whether to extend the suspension ⁠or not.
"Should Tallinn proceed with these plans, our country will take the necessary political and ​diplomatic measures ​in response to ​safeguard its national interests," ‌Zakharova told a press briefing in Moscow.
"Such moves are tantamount to attempts to erect a new Iron Curtain under the false pretence of some sort of threat from the East," ‌Zakharova added.
Estonia, a staunch supporter ​of Ukraine, first announced ​the border closure ​earlier this month, accusing Russia of ‌being behind an attempted ​arson attack ​on drone maker Threod Systems.
The Kremlin denied the accusation at the time, saying it was part ​of what it ‌called a pattern of false allegations against ​Moscow emanating from European countries.
(Reporting by ​ReutersEditing by Andrew Osborn )

articles.content_orig:

Nato scrambled jets on Friday after Poland said its airspace had been violated several times during a Russian attack on Ukraine.
Military aircraft were operating in Polish airspace while ground-based air defences were made ready , the Operational Command of the Polish Armed Forces said in a statement.
“These actions are preventive in nature and are aimed at securing and protecting Polish airspace, especially in areas adjacent to those under threat,” it added.
Poland earlier reported that three objects crossed over from Russia, likely including a KH-101 cruise missile, another missile and a drone.
Defence minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz condemned what he called a “provocation” from Moscow and said he would ask Nato for additional support on its eastern flank.
He assessed that it was unlikely to be a coincidence, occurring as Poland was set to hold military exercises of the 'Coalition of the Willing' of Ukraine's allies on Friday.
Russia’s foreign ministry says it will take ‘necessary measures’ after Estonia said it was closing its border with Russia.
The Baltic country's government said on Friday it would close its road border crossings with Russia on security grounds from December 1 and will decide after six months whether to extend the suspension.
Estonia on Sunday accused Russian security services of staging an attempted arson attack on an Estonian defence company, in what it said was the second such incident this year.
Estonia's northern neighbour Finland shut its Russia border crossings in 2023, and has kept them closed since then, while southern Baltic nations Latvia and Lithuania maintain open crossings.
Polish prime minister Donald Tusk said on Friday that the incursions into Polish airspace do not look like an accident but an “intentional provocation” from Russia.
"We know that what landed on Polish soil came from Russia,” he claimed in a press conference.
“Therefore — and this is not just my own assessment, but also that of our foreign partners, including those within NATO — it does not look like an accident. It appears that we are dealing with an intentional provocation.”
This week repeated Ukrainian strikes have seriously damaged the 19km (12-mile) Crimean Bridge, which straddles the Kerch Strait that links the Black and Azov seas.
The span is vital to sustaining Russia’s military operations, and the £3bn bridge is a potent reminder of Russia’s illegal annexation of the Crimean Peninsula, making it a prime target for Ukraine.
Train traffic stopped after the latest overnight strike into Thursday while authorities assessed the damage, but it resumed in the afternoon, according to Russian state news agency RIA Novosti.
The Ukrainian strikes seemed calculated to embarrass Putin as he met in China with Xi and Trump, as well as to undermine Russia's argument that its victory is inevitable.
In China, Putin insisted the bridge is a civilian asset, adding that he had ordered it closed to carrying military hardware or ammunition.
Putin also said that the road side of the bridge had been “seriously damaged” but vowed to rebuild it. The rail section, which runs parallel to the road, is believed to be stronger in order to bear the greater weight of cargo transport.
Ukraine’s defense ministry said the successful operation to target the bridge meant Russia would need to reroute fuel and ammunition supplies over land, where “our drones are waiting for the cargo.”
The US president should be embarrassed to be rubbing shoulders in this ‘fraternity of autocrats’ with a Russian leader wanted for war crimes by the ICC – but has shown he will stop at nothing for a seat with the ‘big men’ at the table, says Sam Kiley
In China, Trump called Putin “my friend.” The American president’s relationship with Zelensky has soured recently, although the question of US support for Ukraine could be raised by Democrats who will take control of Congress in January after their wins in the midterm elections.
European leaders have tried to isolate Putin diplomatically and have heavily sanctioned the Russian economy as they fear being sidelined by Trump’s direct talks with Putin.
Kushner said that, in his talks with Putin and Xi, Trump “sent a very strong message to both of them on the desire for peace and would like to engage both of them very aggressively to get there.”
He deferred to Trump on giving any details of the “private discussions,” but added: “I believe he also came away believing that peace is achievable and we need to all work together to try and achieve it.”
Putin said in Shenzhen that the Kremlin is not against European participation in talks, but “we need to understand with what Europe will come to these negotiations.” The Kremlin has proposed to European officials through diplomatic channels to come to Moscow “to determine their position,” Putin said, without elaborating. No date has been set.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov declined to say which European officials had been invited or whether Moscow had received a response, Russian state news agency Tass reported.
Polish authorities were investigating reports that at least two unknown objects had come down near the border with Ukraine after the army said Polish airspace might have been violated during Russian strikes on Ukraine.
Authorities in Nato-member Poland said it was too early to say what the objects were. A Ukrainian air force spokesperson said it was likely that a Russian missile had crossed into Poland.
The Russian embassy in Warsaw did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.
Drones have repeatedly strayed into the airspace of countries on Nato’s eastern flank since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, fuelling tension ⁠with the military alliance and stoking fears that the war could spread.
"We confirm the crash of an unidentified object in the village of Nowy Lipowiec," the district prosecutor's office in Lublin wrote on X. "Reports regarding potential additional objects in the region are currently being verified by the relevant services."
Footage shared on ‌social media from what appeared to be a security camera at a property in the nearby village of Chmielek showed an explosion in the distance.
Polish infrastructure minister Dariusz Klimczak said on X that a traffic controller had heard a loud bang near railway premises in Rudnik nad Sanem, about 50km west of Nowy Lipowiec. He said no visible damage to the railway had been found but that an inspection vehicle had been dispatched.
Klimczak also said air traffic controllers had been evacuated at the airport in Rzeszow, the largest city in southeastern Poland.
Prime minister Donald Tusk said he had received reports about security in ​the area and that there was currently no threat from the ‌air.
President Karol Nawrocki was ⁠also informed about the situation.
Vladimir Putin was given a warm reception during the trilateral summit with Trump and Xi. The latest casualty figures are a stark reminder of the devastation the Russian leader has brought to Ukraine, writes James C. Reynolds:
Russian deputy foreign minister ​Sergei Ryabkov on Friday pushed back against the idea of Nato-style security guarantees for Ukraine and said what he called any form of "quasi membership" for Kyiv of the Western military alliance ⁠was totally unacceptable for Moscow, Russian state media reported.
Ryabkov made the comments a day after French president Emmanuel Macron said after a Berlin summit that the question of Ukraine's Nato membership should be reopened. US envoy Jared Kushner said at the same event that he and fellow negotiator Steve Witkoff had "gotten the Russians comfortable with the concept that any security guarantee for Ukraine would be based on Article 5”. articles.title_orig: EU and UK seal reset deal
articles.title_zh: EU and UK seal reset deal
articles.content_orig:
The European Union has struck agreements on three policy areas with the United Kingdom in a move seen as the start of a reset of relations a decade after the Brexit vote.
After a summit in Brussels on Friday, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s office said negotiations have concluded and a reset ⁠deal has been sealed.
“This is a good day for Britain. This is a good day for Europe, and people across Europe and across the United Kingdom will get real benefit,” Burnham had told EU chiefs Ursula von der Leyen and Antonio Costa at the start of the talks.
Downing Street said ‌both sides agreed timelines for implementing a youth mobility scheme, a sanitary and phytosanitary agreement, ⁠and a link ⁠between their emissions trading systems. Details are due ⁠to be published ⁠in a ⁠joint statement.
A UK government spokesperson told Al Jazeera: “The deal is done. Negotiations have concluded. Now both sides will work towards implementation.
“As with all international agreements, there is a legal process in each respective country which will now take place,” the spokesperson added. “And talks will continue on some areas.”
Burnham said the deals could add 0.5 percent to Britain’s economy.
The arrangement to reduce controls on the movement of animals, plants and related products between the UK and EU is worth an estimated 5.1 billion pounds ($6.7bn) to the British economy.
The agreement linking emissions trading systems will exempt British and EU goods, such as steel, from each other’s border carbon levies.
The youth mobility scheme will allow 100,000 young Europeans to live and work in the UK for up to three years, and vice versa.
Despite the agreements, months or years of negotiations lie ahead for a deeper reset in relations to take effect.
Burnham has previously told the British public all options should be on the table for future relations, including rejoining the now-27-nation EU.
However, he has stressed that reversing Brexit is just one possible outcome and far from imminent.
That possibility and the agreements sealed so far will incur anger from the significant section of the British public that remains eurosceptic.
Nigel Farage, leader of the populist right-wing Reform UK party, called Burnham “naive” following the news of the agreements.
The EU has used this moment to “strong-arm the British prime minister”, he claimed. “It’s the same old game, and he’s fallen for it out of sheer inexperience,” Farage wrote on social media.

articles.content_orig:
BH Group’s Isaac Toledano and West Palm Beach developer Kenneth Baboun speak to Fox News Digital about a tech exodus hitting Florida after Anthropic’s record-setting IPO debut.
Now live on the Nasdaq, Anthropic’s $1.5 trillion stock market debut is poised to mint a fresh class of overnight multimillionaires. While Wall Street cheers one of the largest public listings in history, real estate and finance insiders say South Florida is nearing an irreversible "point of no return," as newly liquid tech engineers and institutional backers look to escape high-tax states like California and New York for the Sunshine State’s booming business corridor.
Buying a piece of the IPO action themselves, BH Group CEO Isaac Toledano and West Palm Beach developer and former financial executive Kenneth Baboun are predicting a new tech exodus wave ripping through Florida by mid-to-end of 2027.
"I think we're on the verge of it … People do get tired of being abused, if you will, by your government, not letting you work freely and make money. So I think we're very close to reaching that line that will be a point of no return. We're almost there," Baboun told Fox News Digital.
"Nobody can ignore and forget what Ken Griffin said a few years ago that Chicago's streets are not safe anymore," Toledano also told Fox News Digital. "Everybody wants to follow the smart money, and definitely, it looks like the smart money made the decision that, what we see in South Florida, it's real, and it's here to stay."
INSIDE KEN GRIFFIN'S SECRET THREE-YEAR NEGOTIATION FOR FLORIDA'S LARGEST REAL ESTATE DEAL IN HISTORY
The AI giant and Claude maker’s highly anticipated IPO was priced at $83 per share before beginning trading on Thursday. The listing follows SpaceX’s historic market debut in June, and sets up a massive liquidity event for both early institutional backers and rank-and-file AI engineers once post-IPO lockup periods expire.
Newfound Anthropic IPO wealth could be heading to South Florida, real estate insiders tell Fox News Digital. (Getty Images)
Toledano noted that, after SpaceX’s IPO, a friend who netted $188 million immediately called to buy a luxury condo. Now, Toledano said he’s in active negotiations with a California tech billionaire eyeing a $110 million penthouse at BH Group's newly launched Raffles Residences Coconut Grove.
"The idea behind some of these new millionaires and billionaires [is] keeping some of the money either in stocks, or maybe investing some of their money in real estate, which is a real tangible asset. I think that [people still] learn the lesson from the dot-com days and maybe the financial crisis in 2008, and I think that a lot of people will diversify their investments," Toledano explained.
"We still see buyers coming from California, New York, Chicago, a lot of these blue states," he added.
Baboun noted the excitement around new generational wealth for Anthropic’s workforce and for decentralized investors, believing that Florida is "the best place in the U.S. to be living in" and the best target for potential new residents.
Stuart Varney and Charles Payne discuss the massive wealth creation from the Anthropic IPO. Charles Payne defends the capitalist system, explaining how it raises global living standards and changes lives.
"I do not expect any money from Anthropic to be coming here in the next 45 days that we have left of the year. I do believe next year, as they are able to realize gains, people will be doing some type of tax planning to change their tax residency, and Florida has been very friendly to receive them over here," he said. "What we have seen already in the market has been extreme traffic from California, Texas, Georgia, New York … Since we had the midterms and what happened with that, people are looking into Florida more actively."
The developers and Anthropic stock owners also claimed the market is already seeing heavy migration traffic triggered by recent election cycles and high-tax state policies, creating a further pipeline of demand. Baboun offered that 80% of West Palm Beach buyers still hail from New York and Chicago, California traffic has surged — and buyers who once considered Texas are pivoting to Florida to avoid political and regulatory uncertainty.
"We have a very friendly government that you can come and do business. They don't penalize you for doing business like New York does," Baboun said. "It's really like a perfect storm that we've incubated here."
Toledano agreed, spotlighting the contrast between Republican-backed tax cuts in Florida and rising tax burdens in blue states.
Leaders and attendees at The Real Deal Miami Real Estate Forum speak to Fox News Digital about the passing of Florida’s Amendment 3, which expands homestead exemptions on primary residences.
"I think this is the side effect of the results of the election," he said. "I think that Florida, still being a red state, the state is very active on bringing [in] a lot of companies — companies are still relocating here — pushing real estate taxes down, sending a message to people that while other states pushing their taxes and the real estate taxes up, in Florida, we do exactly the opposite."
According to Barron’s, Anthropic’s IPO filing shows employee stock options alone exceed $100 billion even at the bottom of the pricing range, translating to an average windfall of roughly $20 million per worker, though actual payouts vary by rank and tenure. At the very top, the Bloomberg Billionaires Index previously pegged each of the AI giant’s seven co-founders at an estimated $18 billion fortune based on the IPO's earlier pricing range.
Toledano pointed out that when executives move to Florida, they’re often breaking records on $50 million to $80 million estates in Palm Beach , Coral Gables or Fisher Island, while lower-rank employees can fuel demand for $1.5 million to $3 million waterfront condos in Hollywood and Pompano Beach. Baboun made the assessment that South Florida’s massive post-COVID office construction boom also leaves the commercial market ready for incoming AI firms.
"It's exciting to see other people realize their American dream. It's sad that in parts of this great country, you get penalized for doing that."
"Not all their employees can afford to buy $50 to $60 to $80 million homes in Palm Beach or in Coral Gables or in Coconut Grove. So this is why rentals are still going to do [well] here," Toledano said.
"When we had the pressure of the hedge funds coming down, we were not prepared," Baboun reflected, "but I believe that for this AI and technology boom, we are prepared. We have built more offices than anywhere else in the country."
Critics frequently warn that relying on tech liquidity creates a volatile, speculative housing market that could crash if tech stocks pull back. Toledano rebutted that today’s buyers put down 40% to 50% cash deposits compared to 5% to 10% in 2008, resulting in what he said is a 99.9% closing rate across 800 downtown Miami units he recently delivered.
"[In] the old days, in 2008, 2009, people used to put 5% or maybe 10% deposit, and this is why we saw that big crash. I don't think that this is happening in this cycle," he said.
Taylor Riggs and Brian Brenberg discuss Anthropic raising $81 billion in the biggest initial public offering ever. The AI company's $1.5 trillion valuation officially topples SpaceX's previous $75 billion record.
"Florida cost of life has gone up, but so have incomes," Baboun noted. "Workforce housing [residents] are still making six figures. It's not like they're making $50,000 like they did 10 years back."

articles.title_orig: California investigates Nvidia over whether chip exports ended up in China
articles.title_zh: California investigates Nvidia over whether chip exports ended up in China
articles.content_orig:
State attorney says scandal ‘raises bright red flags’ and aims to find out if company misled investors
California has served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia after a scandal that prompted the departure of co-founder and longtime chief executive Jensen Huang.
Rob Bonta, the US state’s attorney general, issued the subpoena as part of an investigation into whether exports of the California-based company’s advanced semiconductor chips ended up in China, contravening US restrictions.
“The conduct of Nvidia and its former chief executive raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” said Bonta.
“Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: companies cannot mislead their investors.”
The subpoena, issued on Thursday, followed Huang’s resignation a week ago after it emerged he had multiple affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy.
Alice Huang, who is not related, is associated with Singapore-based Megaspeed, which has bought nearly $5bn (£3.8bn) of Nvidia chips and hardware in recent years, and is being investigated for possibly diverting advanced restricted chips to China .
Megaspeed has said it is a “legitimate and lawful” business, and that Huang left the company late last year.
Bonta said the investigation would also look at whether the former Nvidia chief’s actions resulted in confidential information being passed to China.
“My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information,” he said. “And if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law.”
Nvidia’s shares are down by a fifth since Huang admitted the extramarital affair, hitting a one-year low at the close of trading on Thursday, and wiping almost $1tn off its market value.
Earlier this week, Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s chair, said the company had no intention of reinstating Huang after the former CEO said he would be “honoured” to return. Elon Musk and a host of tech bosses had campaigned for Nvidia to bring him back .
Huang is due to testify before several congressional committees over the potential breach of national security on 1 December.
after newsletter promotion
Shares in rival chipmaker AMD closed down almost 8% on Thursday after the publication of reports connected to short seller Hunterbrook warning about its links to China and the “circular financing” of customers.
The company, which has been targeted amid the Nvidia scandal, is looking at a further fall of more than 5% in pre-market trading.
Hunterbrook Media published allegations on the use of AMD’s software by a Chinese server maker blacklisted by the US. Sister publication, The Bear Cave newsletter, alleged that AMD’s use of datacentre lease guarantees and backstops for unsold cloud computing capacity could leave it exposed to a pullback in AI spending.
AMD said the reports’ claims “misrepresent AMD’s business practices and relationships”.
“AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations,” the company said. “We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity.”
AMD’s share price has more than doubled so far this year, giving the company a market capitalisation of more than $800m.

articles.title_orig: An unidentified object appears to have crashed in Poland after Russian attacks in Ukraine
articles.title_zh: An unidentified object appears to have crashed in Poland after Russian attacks in Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Poland says a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace early on Friday and Prime Minister Donald Tusk said it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region.
Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.
Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during one of its biggest aerial attacks on Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022.
Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the Kh-101 missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec in southeastern Poland about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
The cruise missile, designed for precision targets, crashed at about 06:30 (5:30GMT) and Natalie Szponar, a local resident, said she was getting her children ready for school when she heard a "whistle and a dull impact".
Another suspected missile went down near Rudnik nad Sanem to the west of Nowy Lipowiec, and a jet-powered drone crashed to the south near Mołodycz, said Kosiniak-Kamysz.
He called the incursion into Polish airspace a "provocation" from Russia and said he would be asking Nato for additional support.
Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said Nato jets had been scrambled in response. "This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine," he said.
A UK- and France-led exercise called Koalicja 2026 is currently taking place in southeastern Poland involving 11 countries that are part of the West's Coalition of the Willing group in preparation for a potential peace deal in Ukraine.
"It is no coincidence that these objects landed near the site where military manoeuvres by a 'coalition of the willing' supported by Polish troops are taking place in Nowa Dęba," Tusk told reporters on Friday.
The violations of Polish airspace came a day after 40 countries took part in a Coalition of the Willing summit in Berlin, where the allies pledged continued support for Kyiv, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz said peace talks with Russia should take place soon on neutral territory.
At least eight people were killed on Friday as Russian missiles and drones targeted three of Kyiv's bridges across the River Dnipro and a station in Lviv, days after Russia's Vladimir Putin threatened "painful" retaliation for repeated strikes on Russia's bridge across the Kerch Strait to occupied Crimea.
This is not the first time the war in Ukraine has spilled over into Poland and in July a cruise missile also landed in Poland.
