articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Anthropic Stock Drops Premarket as Tech Rout Intensifies
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Anthropic Stock Drops Premarket as Tech Rout Intensifies
articles.content_orig:
Watch: How did Anthropic's stock market debut unfold?
Anthropic has become one of the most valuable public companies in the world after its shares began trading on the stock market, taking its valuation to roughly $1.76 trillion (Â£1.34 trillion).
The artificial intelligence (AI) company's Thursday debut on the Nasdaq stock exchange was a crucial test for the industry, given the huge amount of money being poured into advancing the technology.
Anthropic's shares flew past its allocation price of $83 each , showing there was plenty of excitement around AI.
Yet the company, which is behind AI chatbot Claude, will remain under intense scrutiny in the months ahead to answer the key question surrounding AI: is it all worth it?
In just a few hours of trading, Anthropic's stock seemed to show that investors remain uncertain of where exactly AI is heading. The share price rose immediately to $111.53, sending the company's market value to almost $2 trillion, before falling by the end of the day as the shares closed at $97.17.
Some investors said Anthropic's debut seemed to be a success, as shares rose roughly 17% during the day, but the broader tech market did not perform as well.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index closed down nearly 2.3%. Stocks fell in the largest tech firms, including Google's parent company Alphabet, which was down by 2.9%, while Amazon lost almost 3.9%.
The buildout happening around this era of AI is among the most expensive endeavours in the history of technology, with more than $1 trillion being spent in the last year alone by a handful of major tech companies.
The speed at which investment has grown has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble.
"Bubbles don't burst on the day of the largest deal," Richard Whittle, an economist with the University of Salford said. "They burst later, if the positive future becomes suspect."
Anthropic has made one of the fastest trips from start up to IPO in history
While the basics of the technology have been around for decades, the more recent advent of more powerful computers and related components have allowed the processing of more data than ever.
The result has been AI chatbots that simulate human speech and operate tasks like software coding, digital image generation, and searching the internet more quickly.
It represents a new way of using computers that has led to the rapid rise of Anthropic, which started just five years ago and is best known as the maker of the popular AI chatbot Claude.
As the first purely AI company to go public, Anthropic will almost certainly see significant swings in price on the stock market going forward, according to Ben Barringer, who leads technology research at Quilter Cheviot.
The "initial exuberance" will wear off, Barringer said, pointing to what happened with SpaceX earlier this year.
That company, led by Elon Musk, saw shares jump by about 10% on the first day of trading, taking the company to a record-breaking valuation of $2.2 trillion.
Within a month shares had fallen below their debut price, and have mostly fallen further since.
Most tech companies see their shares fall after hitting the stock market, often after reporting quarterly results for the first time.
But many such companies, including Meta, Amazon and Google, have gone on to become the largest and most profitable corporations in the world.
With Anthropic, investors are not only looking at a notable tech company with a major valuation, and a potentially big future in business, but a company that is the first of its kind on the stock market.
"There's no obvious peer to compare it to," Neil Wilson, an investor strategist at Saxo UK, said.
Simon Jack: Can Anthropic's record-breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting?
Daniela Amodei: Anthropic and the price of AI
So, as individual investors and even researchers and investors at large funds ask themselves if Anthropic is really worth more than $1.7 trillion, or even more, there will be few answers available.
"We'll have a stab at it," Wilson said. "I don't think anyone really knows."
A few things will likely impact the company's success on the stock market in the near-term.
One of those things is the prospect of new laws governing the use of AI tools. In the US, where Anthropic is based, Democrats will be in many more positions of power come 2027, and several politicians have already said they will be looking to ensure AI tools are safe and have some guardrails attached.
Such regulation is currently unlikely at the federal level. US President Donald Trump on Thursday spoke about AI during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China, alongside Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.
Trump reiterated his position against "any form of robust regulation" around the technology, adding, "we won't allow that to happen, frankly."
The same day, however, a bipartisan group of US lawmakers formed the House AI Safety and Innovation Caucus, which will work specifically on AI regulation and safety considerations.
A significant driver of this kind of scrutiny is Anthropic itself. Company executives, including co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei, have been outspoken in their purported fears that future AI tools will become so capable they will outsmart humans, to the point where extinction is possible.
Anthropic has always put itself forward in public as an AI company that takes the safety of its technology very seriously.
Daniela Amodei, Anthropic's president and sister of Dario Amodei, boasted on Thursday that the company "had an AI safety team before we launched our first product".
"AI carries real risks," she added.
Despite the company's claims that the technology it is building at a rapid pace could be dangerous, Anthropic has made one of the quickest trips from start-up to IPO in history.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine strains Russian logistics with Crimean bridge strikes
articles.title_zh: Ukraine strains Russian logistics with Crimean bridge strikes
articles.content_orig:
Russian President Vladimir Putin’s prized Kerch Bridge was struck for the third time this week early on Thursday, halting rail traffic between Russia and occupied Crimea just days after a section of the road bridge collapsed.
As its only direct link to the region, the bridge is strategically important as a military supply artery to Russia. It is also a powerful symbol of Russia’s continued control of Ukrainian territory – as Putin made its construction a key priority after Russia’s illegal annexation of the peninsula in 2014.
The third strike came at a significant moment, as Putin was about to meet US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Asia.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky described previous strikes on the bridge – conducted exclusively with Ukraine-made weapons – as being the seventh stage of what he called “an unprecedented operation in response to Russian strikes on our infrastructure.”
Some rail traffic across the bridge resumed on Thursday afternoon, according to Russia’s transport ministry, which said earlier there were no casualties.
Speaking to reporters in Shenzhen after the unprecedented trilateral meeting in China, Putin threatened Ukraine with “painful” retaliation for the attack. He claimed, despite ample evidence otherwise, that the bridge serves “purely peaceful purposes.”
Kyiv came under a renewed attack from Russian drones on Thursday afternoon. While many were shot down or disabled by Ukrainian air defenses, several got through and struck at the heart of the capital.
Two people were killed in the attack on Kyiv region and five others were injured in the Ukrainian capital, according to authorities.
Projectiles also struck near the embassies of the Netherlands and Austria in Kyiv, according to their governments . Though staff at both embassies were unharmed, the Dutch embassy sustained minor damage, the country’s foreign minister said.
The daytime assault came after Russia launched drone strikes on Ukrainian energy facilities, port infrastructure and vessels overnight. The Russian defense ministry said it hit two power substations in Odesa, a fuel storage facility in Chornomorsk and a cargo ship transporting goods to the port of Odesa. Russia also said it struck a power substation in the northeastern city of Sumy.
The latest attack on the bridge came as Putin was meeting Trump on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, ahead of their historic trilateral talks with Xi.
Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said Putin came out of the meeting in an “excellent mood,” adding that Ukraine was the main topic of discussion, Russian state news agency TASS reported.
Before the meeting, Trump praised his “great relationship” with Putin, calling him “my friend.”
Trump has renewed his push for a negotiated end to Russia’s war on Ukraine in recent months. He has at times been criticized by Kyiv and its European allies of adopting Russian narratives around the war.
Historic three-way talks between Trump, Xi and Putin underway
Meanwhile in Berlin, the so-called Coalition of the Willing – a group of Ukraine’s key allies – convened Thursday with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in attendance.
In a joint press briefing following the meeting, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz emphasized the group’s unwavering support for Kyiv, while British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that progress toward peace had “clearly” been made, adding that Europe “is ready to enter these negotiations.”
Also speaking during the briefing, Kushner said that Trump dialed into the coalition’s meeting and gave his assessment of his talks in Shenzhen. According to Kushner, he conveyed “a very strong message to both of them [Xi and Putin] on the desire for peace and would like to engage both of them very aggressively to get there.”
Zelensky, meanwhile, told reporters in Berlin that how long the war drags on would depend on “the readiness of the US to mediate and pressure (Russia).”
Referring to the trilateral in Shenzhen, Zelensky said both the US and China have the ability to help stop the war.
“If you want to stop Russia, stop trade between Russia and your country — China can do it. The United States can do it. And that’s it. Not enough for their (Russia’s) economy. Not enough for the war.”
The $3.7 billion Crimean Bridge was built to handle 40,000 cars a day and move 14 million passengers and 13 million tons of cargo per year, according to Russian state media.
Ukraine has targeted the Kerch Bridge repeatedly since Russia’s full-scale invasion began in 2022, but the damage the bridge sustained this week appears to be more significant than in some of the previous attacks.
Ukraine has stepped up its attacks on Crimea in the past six months, forcing the Russian-installed authorities to impose a state of emergency over the summer because of widespread power outages and fuel shortages on the heavily militarized peninsula.
This story has been updated with additional developments.
CNN’s Nina Subkhanberdina, Anna Chernova, Victoria Butenko and Arina Porkhovnik contributed to this report.

articles.title_zh: Xi Jinping says a ‘full turnaround’ has been achieved in Australia-China relations, praising Anthony Albanese
articles.content_orig:
US president appeared to doze off while Chinese leader made speech, but White House insisted he was awake
Donald Trump was, again, accused of falling asleep during a televised event, this time during the speech of the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in China.
The US president appeared to close his eyes for roughly 10 seconds on Thursday. As his eyes closed, Trump’s head tilted downward, and his hands remained clasped in front of him.
Several prominent Trump critics on social media alleged that the US president was asleep, including Republicans Against Trump , California governor Gavin Newsom’s press office and conservative lawyer George Conway .
White House officials denied the allegations, claiming the 80-year-old US president was looking down at papers in front of him.
“Fake News! President Trump was looking at papers in front of him while the speaker made remarks. You can clearly see his eyes move back and forth,” Steven Cheung, the White House director of communications, wrote on X in response to a Newsweek article.
“This is why the people despise media so much. They constantly lie,” Cheung added.
Trump often faces accusations of falling asleep during televised events such as Oval Office press conferences, cabinet meetings and sporting events.
Occasionally, while listening to other people speak, the US president will close his eyes for several seconds, appearing as though he is falling asleep . Despite footage of the instances going viral, the White House and Trump allies have insisted the US president does not fall asleep during meetings.
Administration officials have excused Trump’s apparent drowsiness as blinking or an example of the president listening intently. They consistently claim Trump “doesn’t sleep”.
Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, testified to lawmakers earlier this year that he had “never seen” Trump fall asleep.
“On the contrary, the guy doesn’t sleep, which is a big problem because he calls me at two in the morning,” Rubio said in June.
Last year, JD Vance said that Trump hardly ever sleeps, even while traveling overnight.
“If we go on a 20-hour trip somewhere, he doesn’t sleep the entire time. And of course, if he’s not sleeping, if he’s working, he expects everybody else to be working too,” Vance told Fox News .
Trump became the oldest US president ever inaugurated when he was sworn in nearly two years ago. Despite his age, Trump often claims he is in near-perfect health , often bragging about his “perfect” cognitive test results and insisting he has a lot of energy.

articles.title_orig: Quantum Computing Is Even Weirder Than You Think
articles.title_zh: Quantum Computing Is Even Weirder Than You Think
articles.content_orig:
A peer-reviewed study in Science shows the 105-qubit processor demonstrating quantum contextuality from four qubits up to 105
Thu 19 Nov 2026 · 16:35 EST · 4 min read
Google Quantum AI’s Willow processor just won a game that classical computers mathematically cannot win as often. In the four-qubit version of the Mermin-Peres magic square game, Willow posted a 98.3% success rate , clearing the classical ceiling of 88.9%.
That gap is the point. A quantum chip beating a classical strategy at a puzzle sounds like a party trick, but the result is a clean, measurable demonstration of one of quantum mechanics’ strangest properties.
The findings were published on November 19, 2026, in the journal Science , where the work landed on the cover. A preprint version first appeared on arXiv in December 2025, so the peer-reviewed paper arrives roughly a year after the research community first got a look.
Willow itself is a 105-qubit superconducting transmon processor. Google Quantum AI announced the chip in December 2024.
The headline experiment centers on the Mermin-Peres magic square game. Think of it as a cooperative test where players cannot coordinate in real time, yet still need their answers to line up.
Players relying on classical strategies hit a hard cap. Under the research findings, the best they can manage is 88.9%.
Willow reached 98.3%. That is not a rounding-error improvement on the classical limit. It is a result classical logic says should be off the table.
The testing was thorough. The team ran nine game assignments, executing each one 100,000 times.
When Willow did lose, the culprit was mostly residual noise in the hardware. Put simply, the losses came from the chip’s imperfections, not from any flaw in the quantum strategy itself.
Daily. Free. Join 34,000+ readers across crypto, finance, and policy.
We respect your privacy. Unsubscribe anytime.
The property on display here is called quantum contextuality. It means the outcome of measuring a quantum system depends on the experimental context in which you measure it.
The team did not stop at four qubits. They extended the tests to multi-player GHZ-type games and hidden linear function problems, scaling up to all 105 qubits on the chip.
The hidden linear function work relied on a shallow-circuit algorithm. A shallow circuit uses only a few layers of quantum operations, which matters because fewer steps give noise fewer chances to creep in and spoil the result.
Running these tests across the full chip suggests the contextuality advantage is not confined to a small, carefully babysat corner of the hardware. It persisted as the system grew.
One of the more practical takeaways is that the magic square game works as a hardware check. Because the classical limit is fixed and known, any shortfall from the ideal quantum score points to something going wrong on the chip.
The research describes this testing as a way to surface subtle hardware errors. That turns an abstract physics demonstration into something closer to a stress test with a known answer key.
Since most of Willow’s losses traced back to residual noise, the game effectively maps where the remaining imperfections live.
Willow has been Google’s flagship quantum chip since its December 2024 announcement. This latest paper adds a fresh line to its resume, focused less on raw speed and more on proving that the device behaves in genuinely non-classical ways.
The publication timeline is also worth noting. Moving from an arXiv preprint in December 2025 to the cover of Science in November 2026 means the results have now passed formal peer review.
For the quantum computing industry, the result is a credibility marker. Demonstrating contextuality at 98.3% against an 88.9% classical ceiling gives Google a hard number to point to when it argues its hardware does something classical machines cannot.
The scale also matters. Showing quantum behavior across up to 105 qubits, rather than a handful, is the kind of evidence rival labs will likely be measured against.
The research itself acknowledges that practical applications have been slow to roll out, so a winning streak at a logic game is not the same as commercially useful computation.
The more immediate thing to watch is noise. Willow’s losses came largely from residual hardware noise, and how quickly Google and its competitors drive that down will determine whether demonstrations like this one turn into machines that solve problems people will pay for.

articles.title_orig: As Trump courts Xi and Putin, middle powers make their own moves
articles.title_zh: As Trump courts Xi and Putin, middle powers make their own moves
articles.content_orig:
From an airy government villa in the hills of southern China on Thursday emerged an image, perhaps, for our times: the leaders of China, Russia and the US standing shoulder-to-shoulder, proclaiming themselves the stewards of world peace.
For Trump, the moment was a well-timed photo-op – a diplomatic flex for a president who revels in such spectacle and whose party is reeling from a major loss in the US midterm elections.
But for Xi and Putin, the meeting is more likely to go down as a vindication of their vision that the world is undergoing a fundamental rebalancing of power – in their favor.
In opening remarks before the roughly 90-minute meeting between them, Trump said he was honored to sit next to the two and framed the trio – the world’s three largest nuclear powers – as uniquely placed to work together for a “safer future.”
“No problems were ever solved under the old school, refusing to talk about them,” said Trump. “Together, we are choosing a different course.”
But for talks that ended with a handful of vaguely worded outcomes – and no evidence that the US president and commander-in-chief of the world’s most powerful military had tried to hold Putin to account for his illegal invasion of Ukraine – that “different course” appears to be one that plays to the objectives of Moscow and Beijing.
Xi and Putin have long looked to push back against a world order they see as unfairly dominated by the US and its values.
A brief exchange caught on camera in 2023 during a state visit by the Chinese leader to Moscow captures that ambition. There, as he shook Putin’s hand, Xi was heard saying: “Together, we should push forward these changes that have not happened for 100 years.”
To that end, they have tightened their own partnership and built out non-Western international blocs engineered to help usher in a “multipolar” order that favors their interests.
For Xi and Putin, all this is underpinned by a shared view: that the East is rising as the West declines – and the age of American superpower comes to an end.
And what better illustration of that shift than sitting around a table in China’s futuristic tech hub of Shenzhen with a US president hailing them both as friends?
Headlines across Chinese state media the day after the summit were in no doubt about its significance.
The state’s lead news agency hailed the meeting as a “new starting point” for a “new model of relationship among major powers.” That new model, explained the article, is one based on “mutual respect, peaceful coexistence, win-win cooperation, dialogue and consultation.”
For China’s leadership, those are buzzwords key to the country’s unimpeded rise on the global stage, essentially insurance that the US won’t look to meddle in what Beijing sees as its business – especially when it comes to its territorial claims on the self-ruling and democratic island of Taiwan.
And during the summit, with Trump to his left and Putin to his right, Xi pressed that point, using that time, according to Chinese media, to spell out China’s conditions for the three to get along.
At the top of that list? “Respect one another’s sovereignty and territorial integrity” – and stay out of one another’s internal affairs.
For Putin, the meeting was yet another assurance that Trump is taking his concerns into consideration as the US president looks to end Moscow’s war in Ukraine.
Speaking about Trump after the meeting, Putin said, “we have shared certain commonalities in our approaches regarding so-called civilizational values.”
That too, is a buzzword embraced by Putin and Xi, whose vision for a new world order is not one of countries holding each other accountable to universal standards governing rights and political freedoms, but one where countries – and autocrats – are able to set their own rules for their people.
The two leaders will of course be well aware of changing political tides in the US – and the potential that a new Congress in January and a new American president in 2029 could bring immense change to American foreign policy.
Xi and Putin – both shrewd operators who have dominated their countries’ politics for years – will too have calculated they are unlikely to again see another American president as amenable to their interests as Trump.
But that’s what is likely to give this moment even more momentum, as both sides play up the win – and continue their push to reshape global power.

articles.title_orig: Putin scores ‘massive win’ at first trilateral meeting, rebuilding standing as Ukraine war grinds on
articles.title_zh: Putin scores ‘massive win’ at first trilateral meeting, rebuilding standing as Ukraine war grinds on
articles.content_orig:
Russian President Vladimir Putin came away from China stronger than he arrived, standing as an equal beside the leaders of the U.S. and China, both far more powerful than Russia, even as he remains bogged down in a war in Ukraine now in its fifth year.
Putin stood shoulder to shoulder with U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping on a red-carpeted stage Thursday after the first-ever meeting between the three leaders. Trump publicly praised Putin as "my friend" as the two entered a separate bilateral meeting.
Putin was greeted at the APEC summit with smiles and handshakes, and he held bilateral meetings with at least seven world leaders over the two days. This came with the Ukraine war showing no signs of ending, more than four years after Russia invaded its neighbor.
"It's a massive win for Putin," said Joerg Wuttke, an expert at DGA-Albright Stonebridge Group. It's "as if the world has forgiven."
Hours before the three-way meeting, Ukrainian forces struck the bridge linking Russia to Crimea, a peninsula annexed by Russia in 2014, for the third time this week. Russia retaliated with a major attack on Kyiv, killing several people and damaging Ukrainian infrastructure.
The two-day summit appeared to be a symbolic triumph, even as Moscow escalated the war and took a hard line during the European Union leaders' renewed push to end the conflict.
Despite few concrete outcomes, the first-ever three-way summit is "arguably a diplomatic victory for Moscow," said Andrius Tursa, an advisor for Central and Eastern Europe and Russia at Teneo. Putin will likely seek to institutionalize the format, Tursa said.
During the meeting and afterward, Putin and Trump railed against the International Criminal Court, which has had an arrest warrant out for Putin since March 2023. Trump called the court, which his administration has sanctioned, an out-of-control "rogue globalist organization." Putin said he would consider attending the December G20 meeting in Miami after discussing it with Trump.
The three leaders issued a joint declaration of peace after the trilateral talks. Beijing has repeatedly called for negotiations and a political settlement while avoiding condemnation of Russia's aggression.
Putin later spent much of a press briefing after the trilateral meeting defending Moscow's decision to invade Ukraine, insisting that its root causes lie in NATO expansion and the alleged illegitimacy of Ukraine's leadership.
He also blamed the continued conflict on Ukraine's reluctance to accept terms. "If they truly want to end the conflict, they should agree to the compromises ... We accepted those terms; now, it is up to Ukraine."
This stance leaves "little scope for a ceasefire, let alone a durable settlement, absent a material shift in the military balance or political leadership in Moscow or Kyiv," Tursa said.
Russia lags both the U.S. and China in economic clout, population size, and most other major metrics of influence. Russian media, however, portrayed Putin's participation in discussions on global issues alongside the leaders of two major economic and military powers as a recognition of Russia's global power status and a setback for Western isolation efforts.
Putin said that all three leaders agreed that it's a "useful format," and such meetings could take place again.
"A key Kremlin objective will be to institutionalize such a great-power format," said Tursa. No concrete agreements on Ukraine were announced following the summit, and it remains unclear what, if anything, was settled with neither Kyiv nor European officials in the room.
One signal is whether the three leaders meet again in the near future, with the upcoming G20 summit in Miami a potential next opportunity, Tursa said.
Ukraine and European governments have said repeatedly that they must have a say in any talks on their security. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said ahead of the summit that big powers tend to assume they can decide the world's future, which he called a "huge mistake."

articles.title_orig: 4 British Men Convicted of Sexually Assaulting Joanne Young
articles.title_zh: 4 British Men Convicted of Sexually Assaulting Joanne Young
articles.content_orig:
Before Gisèle Pelicot and now Joanne Young, drug-facilitated rape was virtually unheard of. I now realise that my own horrific ordeal was not unique
L ike many, I followed closely the sickening case of Philip Young, who has been convicted of repeatedly drugging and raping his now ex-wife, Joanne Young, and advertising her on the internet for sex. It is, to any right-thinking person, unimaginably horrific that the person you’re supposed to trust most in the world would betray you in this, the worst possible way.
I don’t have to imagine it, however. I have lived it. The man I had been with since I was 17 – my husband and the father of my four children, the man who had vowed to love and look after me and with whom I had shared a bed for almost 7,000 nights – did the same to me.
Since Gisèle Pelicot stepped out of the shadows and waived her right to anonymity, the depraved crime of drug-facilitated sexual abuse has become stamped into the public’s consciousness – rightly provoking outrage and an outpouring of support for survivors.
My experience, some two years before Pelicot’s trial, was different. There was just one single perpetrator, my husband.
I have no idea how many times it happened, nor do I wish to know, but for years he had been crushing sleeping pills into the cup of tea he made for me every night, then waiting for me to lose consciousness before raping me, often taking photographs and filming himself in the act.
There was no outpouring of support when I finally reported the crime . Quite the opposite, in fact. I was ostracised and publicly accused of destroying the reputation of this upstanding pillar of the community. This continued, inexplicably, even after his conviction.
The police were brilliant. The CPS less so. I had to fight to press charges when, after 18 months, it announced it was not going to, even though he had admitted his guilt to medical professionals. I felt as though I was the one on trial rather than him, and the verdict was already in. How could it be true? How could I not have known?
In truth I didn’t, but in hindsight the warning signs had been there: recurrent and unexplained bouts of thrush and urinary tract infections, worsening migraines, and just the nagging feeling that something in my body wasn’t quite right.
The reality was so unimaginable that even when he sat me down and told me what he had been doing, one day after church, it was as though my brain couldn’t process what he was saying. It was months before I told my sister and mum, who gently persuaded me to talk to the police, and it was only then I started to see that what he had been doing – each act – was a crime. A violation of my body, trust and everything I had believed to be true.
It is only recently that I’ve been able to bring myself to call it what it was – rape – and understand (something many survivors struggle with) that just because I can’t remember it, doesn’t mean it didn’t happen. Just because it was my husband doesn’t mean it didn’t count.
I don’t think this type of crime is becoming more common, I think the reporting of it is. The drugs used might be more sophisticated, so, too, the means by which perpetrators communicate with each other and share images and video. The crime, however, has always been there behind closed doors.
Prior to the Pelicot case, this kind of crime was virtually unheard of. What Pelicot did was open the door for people to think that a man could do that to his wife. She created a space in which people could ask questions and could stand up and say, “This has happened to me as well.”
What none of us could have anticipated is the scale. Through #EndEyeCheck , the campaign publicly launched in May this year by fellow survivor-advocate Amanda Stanhope and me, we now know that this has happened and is still happening to hundreds of women around the world – and that doesn’t include those who haven’t yet had that realisation or don’t deem it rape.
The campaign name comes from a term I was blissfully unaware of before all this happened – used to describe the moment an abuser pulls back or lifts the eyelid of their victim to check they are fully unconscious before sexually assaulting them.
after newsletter promotion
Stories such as ours shine a light on this crime, but that is not enough and nor are the sentences handed down. My ex was given 11 years, and I’ll be lucky if he serves the same length of time in prison that his offences span. The government must act now to protect victims.
There needs to be earlier, more effective education around consent, starting in schools, so there can be no confusion and no blurring of boundaries over what is and isn’t allowed. I remember hearing teenage boys on the bus discussing CNC (consensual non-consent) porn and thinking, “Do they even know what it stands for or what it means?”
The platforms, mainstream porn sites among them, that are hosting this almost innocent-sounding “sleep content” must be held to account. It is not innocent – it is perpetuating the idea that consent is not obligatory.
The medical profession and the police also need to be alive to the signs of this type of abuse because the chances are the victims haven’t yet realised what is happening to them and may not, without informed support.
Like many, Pelicot inspired me and played a huge part in the decision to waive my anonymity. It’s not for everyone, but in a strange kind of way it helped me to heal and imagine a future that, at one point, seemed impossible.
It is a complex problem and there is no easy answer, but at least now the conversation has started – and there is a place for women to go for help and to know they are not alone.
Zoe Watts is a campaigner and cofounder of the #EndEyeCheck campaign to raise awareness of drug-facilitated sexual abuse
Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland , or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland . In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html

Valuation expert and New York University professor Aswath Damodaran called Jensen Huang a "great CEO" and said he would buy Nvidia (NVDA) stock if it drops below $140, while also offering a view on the various successor candidates discussed.
"For me, that value is about 30% below my estimated value of $4.8 trillion, yielding a breakeven value per share of around $140 per share, and I have a limit buy waiting at that price," Damodaran said in a new blog post.

"If it happens, I will have Nvidia back in my portfolio, and if it does not, there are other stocks to buy!"
Nvidia's market capitalization has shrunk by more than $2 trillion to $3.52 trillion since Huang first admitted to an affair at the start of last week. Nvidia announced his resignation last Thursday and appointed CFO Colette Kress as the interim chief.
The shakeup has affected the broader AI industry, given that Huang was central to billions of dollars in financing and partnerships with dozens of key AI firms. Nvidia, which is looking for a new CEO, is not out of the woods yet. On Thursday, California launched a probe into whether Nvidia helped China secure advanced AI technology and misled shareholders.
Damodaran cautioned that the stock slide does not automatically make it cheap, saying that "Nvidia's intrinsic value itself has likely dropped due to leadership loss and scandal fallout."
"The wild card in this story is the China twist," Damodaran wrote. If allegations about official Chinese government ties and chip sales through Asian business fronts prove true, the legal and regulatory consequences could persist regardless of who leads Nvidia, he said.
If the disruption from Huang's departure is strictly short-term, such as transition delays, margin pressure, or near-term legal friction, the damage to Nvidia's equity value is contained to a 5% to 10% drop in most scenarios, he said.
However, if Nvidia pulls back on its aggressive customer financing and ecosystem marketing, long-term revenue growth and margins could erode much more severely.
Damodaran said CEO Kress and other insiders are promising candidates, but said Apple CEO Tim Cook "is not a good fit for Nvidia today" unless appointed temporarily to manage a crisis.
"Jensen Huang has been a great CEO, but last week was a reminder that he is human… The essence of corporate governance is that even the very best managers need restraints to prevent overreach, and that giving them complete power in perpetuity is a recipe for regret," he wrote.
NVDA stock is now down 40% from its early-October peak and 21% year to date. On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment for NVDA dipped on Friday but remained in the 'extremely bullish' zone.

By Utkarsh Hathi and Ragini Mathur
Nov 20 (Reuters) - Nasdaq futures fell more than 1% on Friday as Anthropic shares retreated after a blockbuster debut, dashing hopes that the high-profile listing would stabilize an AI trade already shaken by valuation ‌concerns, while hawkish signals from Federal Reserve officials this week also weighed on sentiment.
Anthropic shares slid 7.4% in premarket trading ‌after surging more than 17% on Thursday in their highly anticipated market debut. The stock began trading more than 34% above its offer price of $83.
Anthropic's IPO and ​Nvidia's earnings this week were seen as key tests of whether battered investor confidence in the AI trade could recover.
But neither revived enthusiasm after weeks of concern about the profitability of massive AI infrastructure spending, rising borrowing costs, regulatory risks following Democrats' win in the US midterm elections, and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure.
"Markets are entering a more defensive phase," said Daniela Hathorn, senior market analyst at Capital.com.
"Strong AI demand and successful ‌individual listings are no longer sufficient to sustain ⁠broader risk appetite when investors are questioning valuations, borrowing costs and the outlook for corporate profitability."
As of Thursday's close, the Nasdaq was 13.6% below its October 6 record closing high, while the S&P 500 had ⁠posted its sixth consecutive loss, its longest losing streak since April 2024.
The main US stock indexes were on track for their steepest weekly decline since April 2025, when US President Donald Trump announced Liberation Day tariffs.
Among hyperscalers, Amazon and Microsoft declined more than 1.5% each, while Meta fell 2% ​and ​Alphabet was muted. Amazon and Alphabet are among Anthropic's biggest investors.
Nvidia fell 2.2%, ​while Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom, Marvell, and Micron lost between ‌2.2% and 6.6%.
Neoclouds CoreWeave and Nebius also dropped about 5% each.
Data center stocks IREN, Applied Digital and Core Scientific fell about 4% each.
At 7:03 a.m. ET, Dow E-minis were down 48 points, or 0.1%, and S&P 500 E-minis were down 53.5 points, or 0.74%. Nasdaq 100 E-minis were down 436 points, or 1.64%.
The CBOE Volatility Index, Wall Street's fear gauge, hit the 30-point mark for the first time since March 30.
The selloff in AI-linked stocks has largely overshadowed a strong earnings season.
Of the 462 companies in the S&P 500 to have ‌reported results through Wednesday, 83.5% beat analyst earnings expectations, according to an ​analysis from Tajinder Dhillon, head of earnings and equity research at LSEG Data and ​Analytics.
Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia President Anna ​Paulson said on Thursday the Fed will need to raise interest rates again because inflation is too ‌high, while arguing that shared understanding matters more than explicit ​guidance on the rate outlook.
Markets are ​pricing in a 98.4% chance of an interest rate hike from the central bank at its next meeting in December, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool.
Next week's personal consumption expenditures (PCE) figures will provide further clarity on the Fed's monetary policy path ​after a hotter-than-expected October inflation report last ‌week.
Among other movers, Intuit shares fell 9.7% after the company cut its annual revenue growth forecast and agreed to sell ​Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for about $3.68 billion, five years after acquiring it for nearly three times as much.
(Reporting by ​Utkarsh Hathi and Ragini Mathur in Bengaluru; Editing by Maju Samuel)

Chinese technology firms are bracing for impacts on their ambitious artificial intelligence plans as the U.S. tightens restrictions on China 's access to the world's cutting-edge chips.
Chinese tech giant Alibaba , which on Thursday announced another quarter of strong revenue growth for its global AI cloud and compute services, warned that the new U.S. rules could affect some of its global data center expansion plans. It said it was still assessing the repercussions.
The Trump administration this week issued new rules in the wake of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation, following the news that he’d had an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.
The rules now restrict remote computing access through data centers in third countries, the latest U.S. move to curtail China’s abilities to use advanced Nvidia chips to train its increasingly capable AI models.
Alibaba's AI revenues are surging as demand grows
As the technology race between the two superpowers intensifies, existing U.S. export restrictions already barred China from getting the world’s most powerful chips.
But some Chinese companies have been able to bypass those restrictions by renting remote computing access to train AI models, pushing the U.S. to close what some policymakers called a loophole.
As global AI usage grows, Alibaba has been expanding its capabilities across chips, cloud infrastructure and AI models. It launched its flagship Qwen4-Max AI model earlier this week. In September, Alibaba's CEO called its new Zhenwu V900 chip the “most powerful” AI chip in China, while it announced massive data center investment plans in China and abroad.
Alibaba Cloud’s AI-related revenue currently comes significantly from China and there’s still a lot of “untapped demand” from Chinese enterprises, said Jacob Cooke of the Beijing-based consultancy WPIC Marketing + Technologies.
For the latest July-September quarter, Alibaba reported a 53% year-on-year revenue surge for its AI cloud and compute services to nearly 61 billion yuan ($9 billion). Total revenue for the quarter rose 10% from the year before to almost 272 billion yuan ($41 billion), slightly better than what analysts had expected.
While the company has a strong cash buffer, capital expenditures jumped 60% during the quarter to 50.5 billion yuan ($7.6 billion) thanks to its increased spending on AI infrastructure buildout.
Tencent says US chip curb ‘sets everyone back in China’
Chinese tech giant Tencent on Wednesday said the new U.S. rule on chip access “sets everyone back in China.”
“Everyone is actually having less compute, advanced compute, to work with, no matter when you actually started leasing or building capacities outside of China,” Tencent President Martin Lau said on an earnings call. Training timelines for Tencent’s next versions of its AI models would probably be impacted, he said.
“Chinese AI firms are still heavily dependent on the most frontier Nvidia chips," said James Chai, a researcher at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore, with new U.S. rules on remote access cutting off a huge portion of Chinese firms’ access to compute.
A study released in October by the Institute for Progress, a U.S. think tank, estimated that remote access to AI chips through overseas data centers could account for roughly one-third of China’s AI compute by the end of 2027.
Nvidia, meanwhile, said it is now “no longer shipping” chips including the H200, one of its more powerful chips, though not the most advanced, although the Trump administration greenlighted some sales to China, reflecting how Nvidia has toughened its stance on China following Huang’s ouster.
Analysts expect the U.S. will step up its chip export control policies against China after Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a former senior executive of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, raised U.S. national security concerns. Earlier reporting by The New York Times suggested that U.S. officials suspected Alice Huang was a Chinese spy recruited in part to potentially influence Nvidia to make its most advanced chips more available to Chinese companies.
Beijing has rejected claims that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy, and has called the new U.S. rules blocking Chinese companies' remote access to computing power overseas “economic coercion.”
Analysts and industry leaders in China say the U.S.’s tightening of chip export control measures would ultimately accelerate China’s push to make its domestic chip industry self-sufficient.
“Over the longer run, we believe all Chinese players would actually have to rely on domestic supply chains and domestic chips, which we actually see the industry is actually progressing very fast,” said Tencent's Lau.

MANAMA, Bahrain — Conferences in the Persian Gulf are usually positive affairs, with government officials, executives of state-owned companies and armies of consultants touting petro-fueled visions promising fantastical technology and prosperity.
Yet optimism seemed in short supply at the Manama Dialogue, an annual security and geopolitical summit held in the Bahraini capital. Instead, the dominant mood among the Middle East diplomats, defense officials and experts assembled last weekend was fear over the consequences of another bout of U.S.-Iran fighting.
“The rules of logic tell us that the Iranian stand and the American stand are far apart. And if these positions are not bridged, then we have to worry about the worst,” Anwar Gargash, a presidential advisor in the United Arab Emirates, said in an address at the summit.
Gargash added that it’s not in the interest of the regional countries or Iran to go through another round of war.
“While we’re going through this period of protracted crisis of no war, no peace, we are clearly seeking a political offramp,” he said.
In his address, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said, “We have to push very hard in order to prevent the escalation.”
Noting that more fighting would affect food and energy security, he added, “The second round will be more dangerous, more destructive and it will lead to nowhere.”
The signals from Washington are mixed.
With a settlement between Tehran and Washington seemingly out of reach, President Trump has hinted he could launch “another little Operation Epic Fury” after Tuesday’s midterm elections. He was referring to the U.S.-Israeli operation that launched the war on Iran on Feb. 28.
But on Monday, he wrote on his social media website that “Iran wants a settlement, as soon as possible. It could happen!”
Still, hours later, Iranian state media reported explosions on Iran’s Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz; the Associated Press quoted an unnamed U.S. official as saying the military had carried out “defensive strikes.”
The news comes as Republicans face a tough midterm race, which has become a referendum on an increasingly unpopular war that could sink Trump’s Teflon-like electoral appeal.
Iran has expanded its threats but says it is awaiting the latest U.S. response. The latest proposal Iran has publicly discussed would fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz to shipping within two days if Washington meets several conditions, including lifting its blockade of Iranian ports.
Meanwhile, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is fighting for his political life after an inconclusive election last month, is said to be pressing Trump to finish off the Islamic Republic.
Behind the scenes, regional diplomats are engaging in furious shuttle diplomacy to avert renewed fighting. Last week, Saudi, Pakistani and Turkish officials flew to Tehran and met with Iranian military officials. Qatar is leading negotiations between the U.S. and Iran, with Tehran presenting  a de-escalation plan that has yet to be accepted by Trump.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Monday told the state-run Islamic Republic News Agency that it was now up to the Americans to decide “whether they have the will to take the wise path of diplomacy or, as in the past, seek to drag the situation into aggression and military operations.”
“If they dare to test us again,” he added, “they know that they will receive a much more bitter and severe result than before.”
His words came as several Middle Eastern countries are still reeling from the first round of fighting, when Iran retaliated against U.S. attacks by striking American military bases on regional soil with fusillades of drones, as well as cruise and ballistic missiles.
Iran also targeted civilian infrastructure and has vowed to exercise less restraint and wage a no-holds-barred campaign — possibly striking energy, desalination and travel facilities — in the event of a new assault.
On Saturday, Iran’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, said further U.S. attacks would prompt a broad response, one without “geographic limits.”
The scars of the fight could be seen around the Bahraini capital, where the U.S. 5th Fleet has several support facilities. Structures showed signs of explosive damage, including a partially destroyed radar dish and soot-covered depot, a result of Iranian projectiles — 500 drones and roughly 200 ballistic missiles — finding their mark.
The bases seemed all but abandoned, with word among residents that American service members, a common sight in Bahrain, have all but disappeared.
The war has cast a shadow on Persian Gulf nations that have long presented themselves as paragons of stability in a volatile region, mostly unaffected by the conflicts raging in the wider Middle East.
Disruptions to energy flows and logistics mean members of the Gulf Cooperation Council, or GCC, a bloc of oil-rich Gulf nations, are facing a 4.8% contraction in gross domestic product compared with last year, according to the International Monetary Fund.
The International Monetary Fund expected a strong turnaround in 2027 but acknowledged that “uncertainty remains exceptionally high, and risks are firmly tilted to the downside.”
Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar are hardest hit; Qatar’s real GDP is down more than 15% this year. Meanwhile, the Saudi economy — which is contending with the double pressures of a sealed-off Strait of Hormuz and a blockade on Red Sea access by Iran-backed Yemeni rebels known as the Houthis, shrank almost 4% in the third quarter compared with last year, according to official figures.
Despite regional efforts to bring about a detente, the general consensus among attendees at the security summit  was that more war is coming. The summit, which is organized by the International Institute for Strategic Studies think tank, drew hundreds of participants.
And for both regional and European officials present, there was a deep sense of uncertainty regarding Washington and its commitment to shielding putative allies from attack.
That has forced Gulf nations — long reliant on a U.S. security umbrella — to look for protection beyond Washington. Yet diplomats lamented what they said was a lack of coordination close to home, despite a long-standing GCC mutual defense agreement.
The U.S.-Israeli war on Iran and conflict with the Iran-backed Houthis of Yemen have unsettled Saudi Arabia, a kingdom unused to conflicts playing out on home turf.
For example, militaries detecting projectiles in their airspace that were en route to a target country didn’t warn their counterparts, leaving them with less time to deal with incoming attacks. Others have systems that are not linked to the U.S.’s regional radar net.
“A lot of countries you thought you can depend on were not there for you,” Gargash said. “Why did we sign that agreement many years ago only to see that this agreement was not activated when we all needed it?”
Saudi Arabia has sought to marshal alternative allies through a recently signed pact with Turkey and Pakistan, and has asked Egypt for help — a request Cairo said it would honor by engaging in defensive operations on Saudi territory.
But Abdelatty, Egypt’s foreign minister, said the region requires more than new military engagements and should instead “move from the logic of crisis management to the logic of building an order” aimed at stopping confrontations before they start.
“A war can begin with a unilateral decision,” Abdelatty said.
“But no one can unilaterally control its consequences or stop it.”

articles.title_orig: Hours after Trump reportedly says ‘tired’ Putin is ready for a deal, Ukraine hit with massive strikes
articles.title_zh: Hours after Trump reportedly says ‘tired’ Putin is ready for a deal, Ukraine hit with massive strikes
articles.content_orig:
Moscow launched a deadly missile and drone attack on Ukraine overnight into Friday, just hours after Russian President Vladimir Putin met his US and Chinese counterparts for historic trilateral talks in which the three powers billed themselves as a force for peace in the world.
Trump spoke to European leaders after the call, reportedly describing Putin as “tired” and ready for peace. But Kyiv said Russia fired at least 110 missiles overnight - an unusually large number even amid Russia’s frequent aerial assaults.
Eight people have been killed and at least 28 injured during the massive attack which has so far lasted more than eight hours, according to Ukrainian authorities.
Some 400 drones, including 120 jet-powered drones which are essentially compact cruise missiles, were also part of the attack.
The Polish government said on Friday that fighter jets were scrambled and Patriot air defense systems activated early on Friday after Poland’s airspace was violated during the attack, with “objects” flying in and falling inside the country’s territory.
The deadly assault came hours after Putin left China following a day of meetings in Shenzhen with US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping.
The talks failed to produce any breakthrough on Moscow’s more than four-year war in Ukraine, and appeared to be used by Putin as an opportunity to repeat his maximalist demands and false narratives about the conflict in front of a global audience.
The Russian leader hailed the summit with Xi and Trump as historic and told reporters the discussions took place in a “relaxed and very intimate atmosphere.”
In his opening remarks, Putin said Russia, China and the US have “shared interests” in settling the Ukraine war.
No official declaration or a readout were released after the talks, but Trump did speak afterwards to the so-called Coalition of the Willing, a group of Ukraine’s key allies which was convening with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Berlin.
According to a senior European official with knowledge of the call’s contents, the president’s main message was that “Putin is tired, wants to end this, ready for a deal.”
The official said Trump’s suggestion was “to reach out and grasp at the opportunity.”
He said the Europeans were “constructive in response but want proof.”
Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk, who was part of the call, said that Trump sounded “fairly optimistic.”
“Although I have to say (his words) were received very cautiously in the room, when it comes to Putin’s and Moscow’s intentions regarding peace talks.”
“But I don’t hide the fact that I’ve heard this very often from President Trump. His belief in Putin’s goodwill seems unshakable, even though so far there are no facts to support it, he said, adding that it “would be good, if it really turned out that Russia was genuinely ready to engage in peace talks.”
Kushner said Trump had conveyed “a very strong message to both of them [Xi and Putin] on the desire for peace and would like to engage both of them very aggressively to get there.”
Russia’s defense ministry said in a post to Telegram it launched a “massive strike using high-precision weapons from land, sea, and air,” as well as drones, targeting Ukrainian military and energy facilities, port infrastructure in the Odesa region, and transport infrastructure in Kyiv.
But Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky said “a bsolutely all the targets were ordinary civilian infrastructure – things that literally sustain people’s lives.”
“This was one of the largest attacks. The strike tactics were particularly vicious this time: several groups of missiles were launched, with pauses of 20 to 30 minutes between them to make it harder to put out fires, clear rubble, and carry out repairs,” Zelensky said.
Zelensky said that 27 of the missiles
Earlier, Ukraine said Moscow’s targets included a hospital in Kharkiv and residential buildings in the Dnipropetrovsk, Lviv, Vinnytsia, Sumy, and Chernihiv regions.
Three of Kyiv’s bridges were damaged in the overnight strikes, according to mayor Vitaly Klitschko, halting transport links connecting the two sides of the capital.
“All emergency services have done and will continue to do everything possible to mitigate the consequences of the attack as quickly as possible,” Klitschko said, adding that people should avoid traveling if possible.
The deadly attack came after Putin vowed revenge for Ukraine’s recent attacks on prized project, the strategic multibillion-dollar bridge linking Russia with the occupied Crimea.
“There will be no negotiations,” he said. “I believe our response, as I have just said, will be far more painful than what the Kyiv regime did to the bridge.”
The attacks have also knocked down power in several regions across Ukraine, just as temperatures are beginning to drop to bellow zero.
Several districts in Kyiv were without power due to the attack, according to energy company DTEK. Emergency power outages have also been implemented in the Lviv, Zakarpattia, and Ivano-Frankivsk regions, according to Ukrenergo, the country’s state-owned electricity operator, which called the situation in the power grid “extremely critical.”
CNN’s Nick Paton Walsh and Victoria Butenko contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: For Xi and Putin, the Trump trilateral was a win for a new world order
articles.title_zh: For Xi and Putin, the Trump trilateral was a win for a new world order
articles.content_orig:
From an airy government villa in the hills of southern China on Thursday emerged an image, perhaps, for our times: the leaders of China, Russia and the US standing shoulder-to-shoulder, proclaiming themselves the stewards of world peace.
For Trump, the moment was a well-timed photo-op – a diplomatic flex for a president who revels in such spectacle and whose party is reeling from a major loss in the US midterm elections.
But for Xi and Putin, the meeting is more likely to go down as a vindication of their vision that the world is undergoing a fundamental rebalancing of power – in their favor.
In opening remarks before the roughly 90-minute meeting between them, Trump said he was honored to sit next to the two and framed the trio – the world’s three largest nuclear powers – as uniquely placed to work together for a “safer future.”
“No problems were ever solved under the old school, refusing to talk about them,” said Trump. “Together, we are choosing a different course.”
But for talks that ended with a handful of vaguely worded outcomes – and no evidence that the US president and commander-in-chief of the world’s most powerful military had tried to hold Putin to account for his illegal invasion of Ukraine – that “different course” appears to be one that plays to the objectives of Moscow and Beijing.
Xi and Putin have long looked to push back against a world order they see as unfairly dominated by the US and its values.
A brief exchange caught on camera in 2023 during a state visit by the Chinese leader to Moscow captures that ambition. There, as he shook Putin’s hand, Xi was heard saying: “Together, we should push forward these changes that have not happened for 100 years.”
To that end, they have tightened their own partnership and built out non-Western international blocs engineered to help usher in a “multipolar” order that favors their interests.
For Xi and Putin, all this is underpinned by a shared view: that the East is rising as the West declines – and the age of American superpower comes to an end.
And what better illustration of that shift than sitting around a table in China’s futuristic tech hub of Shenzhen with a US president hailing them both as friends?
Headlines across Chinese state media the day after the summit were in no doubt about its significance.
The state’s lead news agency hailed the meeting as a “new starting point” for a “new model of relationship among major powers.” That new model, explained the article, is one based on “mutual respect, peaceful coexistence, win-win cooperation, dialogue and consultation.”
For China’s leadership, those are buzzwords key to the country’s unimpeded rise on the global stage, essentially insurance that the US won’t look to meddle in what Beijing sees as its business – especially when it comes to its territorial claims on the self-ruling and democratic island of Taiwan.
And during the summit, with Trump to his left and Putin to his right, Xi pressed that point, using that time, according to Chinese media, to spell out China’s conditions for the three to get along.
At the top of that list? “Respect one another’s sovereignty and territorial integrity” – and stay out of one another’s internal affairs.
For Putin, the meeting was yet another assurance that Trump is taking his concerns into consideration as the US president looks to end Moscow’s war in Ukraine.
Speaking about Trump after the meeting, Putin said, “we have shared certain commonalities in our approaches regarding so-called civilizational values.”
That too, is a buzzword embraced by Putin and Xi, whose vision for a new world order is not one of countries holding each other accountable to universal standards governing rights and political freedoms, but one where countries – and autocrats – are able to set their own rules for their people.
The two leaders will of course be well aware of changing political tides in the US – and the potential that a new Congress in January and a new American president in 2029 could bring immense change to American foreign policy.
Xi and Putin – both shrewd operators who have dominated their countries’ politics for years – will too have calculated they are unlikely to again see another American president as amenable to their interests as Trump.
But that’s what is likely to give this moment even more momentum, as both sides play up the win – and continue their push to reshape global power.

articles.title_orig: China revels in Xi Jinping’s ‘Yalta 2.0’ moment
articles.title_zh: China revels in Xi Jinping’s ‘Yalta 2.0’ moment
articles.content_orig:
President Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin sat down together in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday in a rare face-to-face encounter for the leaders of three of the world's most powerful countries, but there appeared to be little concrete to show for the meeting in terms of resolving any of the crises facing the world.
The leaders offered a joint statement after their roughly hour-and-a-half-long meeting. Mr. Trump immediately left for his return flight to the U.S. without speaking to journalists on the ground. On the flight home, the president said on social media he will hold a press conference at noon on Friday to discuss the trip.
The presidents discussed Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine , which Mr. Trump has wanted to bring to a negotiated end. But the only significant statement on the conflict came after the meeting from Putin, who ruled out any direct negotiations with Ukraine, citing a major strike earlier this week by Ukrainian forces on a key bridge in Russian-held Crimea.
Putin's senior aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters after the meeting that the atmosphere had been good, and the Kremlin quickly released what it called a joint statement from all three leaders characterizing the talks. The White House later provided the same statement.
The three men "exchanged views in detail on the current international situation and reaffirmed their commitment to maintaining strategic stability and international security," the readout said, adding that as permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, they had "reaffirmed their commitment to reforming the UN so that it can more effectively respond to global challenges and fulfill its fundamental mission in the area of international peace and security."
They also committed to increasing gas and oil production "for the benefit of all countries," agreed on the "fundamental importance" of "the principle of state consent and respect for the immunities of state officials," and said the " International Criminal Court and other similar bodies should not abuse their powers."
Finally, the leaders "reaffirmed that there can be no winners in a nuclear war, and that it should never be unleashed."
The White House indicated that Mr. Trump might speak with reporters on Air Force One during the flight back to the U.S.
The Kremlin shared a short video on social media, via Russian state media, showing Xi accompanying Putin as they walked out of the meeting to Putin's waiting motorcade. Before they exit the building, Putin is seen shaking Xi's hand, thanking him for hosting the gathering and telling him, according to Russian state media, that nobody had expected it to go so well.
Before the meeting, Mr. Trump met separately with Putin on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, and then with Xi.
"We've had a great relationship for many years," Mr. Trump said, standing alongside his Russian counterpart. "I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start."
As Mr. Trump approached Putin for a handshake, he said, "Who is that?" before laughing and saying, "He's my friend."
Democratic Sen. Tim Kaine, who sits on the Committee on Foreign Relations, said the image of Mr. Trump standing with Xi and Putin was concerning.
"Some of the pictures troubled me, seeing the president stand with Putin and Xi, rather than seeing the president stand with the leaders of the global democracies," Kaine said. "When I saw them, it turned my stomach a bit, and particularly President Trump's declaration that Vladimir Putin was a friend. Vladimir Putin is not a friend, and so you know he was either being insincere or he is deeply deluded if he thinks Vladimir Putin is a friend."
In a phone call with NBC reporter Gabe Gutierrez, Mr. Trump called the meeting a 12 on a scale of zero to 10.
Russia's TASS news agency said the war in Ukraine was the main topic discussed by the two leaders, and that Putin left the meeting in "an excellent mood."
After the trilateral talks Thursday, Putin told reporters that Ukraine and Europe were "not yet ready" to make the compromises necessary to resolve the war, according to Russian media.
"We will not negotiate after the attacks on the Crimean bridge," he declared, referring to this week's Ukrainian strike on the highly symbolic Kerch Bridge, which links Russia with Ukraine's Russian-occupied Crimean Peninsula.
Putin said Kyiv and Europe would eventually come to understand that it is better to make compromises than to face "realities."
Ukraine and its European partners have long feared that the White House appears willing to offer Putin too much — including the prospect of major energy deals — with no significant concessions from Russia  in return, while putting pressure on Kyiv to make major territorial concessions without any concrete security guarantees.
Mr. Trump then met for about an hour with Xi ahead of the three-way meeting. As the Trump-Xi session began, Xi told Mr. Trump relations between China and the United States were "stable and improved."
Mr. Trump told reporters he had spoken with Xi for two hours on Wednesday, with trade and tariffs being the main topics. He also said he would be asking China to "do some more" for American farmers, because China has an "insatiable appetite."
Mr. Trump said previously that he planned to talk about denuclearization with his fellow leaders. Russia and the United States are by far the world's largest holders of nuclear weapons , with stockpiles estimated at well over 5,000 warheads, while China is believed to be a distant third, with about 600 weapons.
Putin has made denuclearization a key talking point for decades, but both he and Mr. Trump have allowed previous treaties intended to limit nuclear proliferation to lapse in recent years. China, which has been building up its nuclear program , ruled out taking part in any denuclearization talks with the U.S. and Russia as recently as last year .
China's state-run Xinhua news agency quoted Xi , however, as saying ahead of the trilateral meeting on Thursday that nuclear weapons were a "sword of Damocles hanging over humanity," and calling for them to be "completely banned and completely destroyed, leading to a world free of nuclear weapons."
The Kremlin said in its readout of the three-way meeting that it would "continue dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons" with China and the U.S.
A range of other global challenges lingered in the background of the trilateral meeting, including the war in Iran and tension over trade and artificial intelligence .
The summit took place in the capital of the Chinese tech industry, a sector that has drawn intense scrutiny in recent weeks amid worries that advanced U.S. computer chips are surreptitiously reaching China. The scandal was sparked by allegations that now-former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a businesswoman and suspected Chinese intelligence asset, Alice Huang , whose company is accused of diverting Nvidia's coveted AI chips to China. Beijing has dismissed claims that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy as "groundless speculation" and "nothing more than an attempt to smear China."
Mr. Trump — an ally of Jensen Huang's — had previously told reporters he may bring up the businesswoman during his meetings in China, though he said, "I don't know that she is a spy." Her firm, Megaspeed , is under Justice Department investigation. It has denied wrongdoing.
Shortly after the concerns about Jensen Huang surfaced, the Trump administration issued a new rule aimed at curbing China and other countries' ability to remotely access advanced AI chips. China and the U.S. have also discussed broader AI policy issues in recent months, including setting up a communication channel to share information when AI systems go haywire.

articles.title_zh: White House pool have phones taken away on return from China as speculation mounts over unscheduled stop
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
White House reporters traveling aboard Air Force One had their phones temporarily confiscated before President Donald Trump’s plane took off after his trilateral summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, raising the specter of an unscheduled detour on his way back to Washington D.C.
U.S. officials collected reporters’ devices as the president’s plane prepared to leave Shenzhen, China, Thursday evening.
“At 6:45 pm consider this your wheels up,” the White House pool report read. “Our phones are being taken away for now for security reasons.”
No one on the trip has provided more information. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for more information.
It is highly unusual for reporters’ phones to be sequestered outside of situations when the president is traveling to a war zone, such as when Trump flew to Al Asad Air Base in Iraq at Christmas in 2018, and to Bagram Air Field in Afghanistan for Thanksgiving in 2019.
Fox News correspondent Jacqui Heinrich, the current president of the White House Correspondents’ Association, pointed out on X that the pool’s phones were not taken when Trump left Beijing after his state visit in May.
The move was later explained as a cybersecurity measure, as the phones used by journalists in China were placed in a metal-lined Faraday bag to prevent them from emitting any signals while the aircraft was aloft.
Most of the devices that were collected were so-called burner phones used only for the travel to China, as journalists had previously stored their regular devices in similar bags aboard Air Force One for use during the Philippines leg of the trip and while en route to Washington.
Separately, a flight restriction that had been imposed over Alaska around the time Air Force One had been scheduled to refuel there was lifted Thursday, raising questions as to the plane’s destination.
The most obvious candidate for a detour was North Korea. Trump spent the days before the summit musing that Kim Jong Un might join him when he met with China ’s Xi and Russia ’s Putin on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.
On Wednesday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters in Manila that the president was “prepared” to meet the North Korean leader.
“It may not happen, but he’s prepared to do it,” Rubio said.
However on a call with reporters before the trip, senior U.S. officials said there were “no plans at all for engagement with North Korea.”
Trump relished the pageantry and attention that were lavished on his first two meetings with Kim, though neither sit-down resulted in the denuclearization deals he had promised to reach with the brutal autocrat.
He also met Kim for a third time during a visit to the Korean Demilitarized Zone and briefly became the first American president to set foot in North Korea.
The intrigue surrounding the president’s departure from China followed Trump’s participation in the first-ever meeting between an American president and the autocrats who have led the other two major nuclear powers for a combined 41 years.
Trump gave Putin a warm reception when he met with him for a bilateral meeting immediately preceding the three-way sit-down.
The U.S. president pointed, smiled and called out “Who is that? He’s my friend!” as he walked into a room with his Russian counterpart. The scene was captured by TV cameras that had been permitted in, even as journalists were barred from attending to prevent the leaders from being asked any uncomfortable questions, though a Russian official attributed the move to space constraints.
Trump said of Putin: “We’ve had a great relationship for many years. We know each other for a long time, and I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start. But I think they’ll come out of this.”
The Kremlin said after the meeting that the pair had discussed the ongoing war in Ukraine , and that Putin left in an “excellent” mood.
The White House offered no official readout of the sit-down, which lasted approximately 40 minutes.
Following the trilateral meeting, the Russian, Chinese and American governments released a four-point “peace declaration” reaffirming that a nuclear war should never be fought and vowing to engage in dialogue on reducing nuclear risks.
The three leaders also pledged to advance reforms of the United Nations, to increase supplies of refined petroleum products for all countries and to uphold the immunity enjoyed by state officials in international courts.
The International Criminal Court in The Hague has issued arrest warrants for Putin and five other Russian officials. The Trump administration has been working to delegitimize and defund the ICC out of fear that Trump and his associates could be subject to war crimes charges over America’s campaign of airstrikes against alleged drug smugglers or an airstrike against an Iranian school that left over 100 children dead.

articles.title_orig: Asian Equities Tumble as AI Stock Selloff Deepens
articles.title_zh: Asian Equities Tumble as AI Stock Selloff Deepens
articles.content_orig:
Asian markets on track for their worst week since 2020, with European and US stocks also way down
Business live – latest updates
Global stock markets have slumped as Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a sell-off in AI-linked companies.
Asian stock markets were on track for their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell on Friday. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chip maker TSMC down about 6%.
In Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI.
European stock markets were heading for their worst week since March, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.3% in the first 90 minutes.
The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by more than 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO .
Anthropic’s shares jumped by 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the frontier AI firm began. But they were heading for losses on Friday, down 6% at $91.30, falling back towards the IPO price of $83.
Anthropic’s flotation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI build out.
Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending.
“The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.”
after newsletter promotion
Britain’s FTSE 100 share index hit a five-month low on Friday morning. It has dropped by 4.8% this week, and is heading for its biggest weekly fall since the start of the Iran war.
